Paper yellows: lignin oxidises, sizing degrades, and blue dyes are among the least lightfast materials in the room. So these works have themselves travelled from summer to autumn, in the same direction as their subject, over a century, in storage.

This is not a footnote for conservators. It changes the reading. A Sisley pastel that today looks like a warm October afternoon may have been drawn as a cold one, its greys held up by a blue support that no longer exists. Anyone measuring a faded pastel is measuring two events at once: the light the artist saw, and the hundred and twenty years since.
Autumn begins on the seventh of August

Everything above assumes that a season is a lighting condition, something you detect by looking at the sky and the ground. One tradition organises it the other way round, and holding the two side by side is the fastest way to see that the European nineteenth century made a choice rather than a discovery.

In the Japanese calendar inherited from China, the year is divided into twenty-four solar terms, and the one called risshu, the beginning of autumn, falls around the seventh or eighth of August. Not the equinox, not the first cold night: the seventh of August, when the heat in Kyoto is at its worst. Autumn is declared. From that date onward a poem that mentions cicadas, dew, geese or the moon is an autumn poem, whatever the thermometer says, and a painter who signs a screen of grasses in September is working inside a season that officially began five weeks earlier.

The terms are then subdivided again, into seventy-two ko of roughly five days each, every one named after a single natural event. The Japanese set was revised into its familiar form by the court astronomer Shibukawa Shunkai in the seventeenth century. The three that make up risshu are, in order: cool winds arrive, evening cicadas sing, thick fog descends. A month later, under white dew, comes the unit called dew glistens white on the grass.

This deserves attention from anyone who has just read four thousand words of measurements. It is the same instinct, an attempt to resolve the turn at the finest grain available, but the instrument is a name rather than a number, and the resolution is five days rather than a hue percentage. The tradition that supposedly does not measure the season has divided it into units so short that most European calendars have no word for them at all.
The season is a plant, not a light

If autumn is a date rather than a condition, then a picture cannot announce it by the angle of the sun, and it does not try to. It announces it with a plant. The Man'yoshu, the eighth-century anthology, fixes the seven grasses of autumn in a pair of poems by Yamanoue no Okura: bush clover, miscanthus, kudzu, pink, patrinia, boneset, bellflower. For the next twelve hundred years those seven, and above all the miscanthus called susuki, carry the season in poetry, on lacquer, on ceramics and across screens.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgt0vbnygt0f4.jpg
content.caption: Susuki Grass, about 1525. One of a pair of six-panel folding screens; ink, colour and gold on paper, 150.4 by 349.2 cm. Cleveland Museum of Art, John L. Severance Fund, CC0.

content.content: This screen is three and a half metres of one plant. There is no ground line, no horizon, no sky, no cast shadow, no hour of the day. Measured, the green pigment covers 2.4 per cent of the surface: the remaining ninety-seven and a half per cent is the prepared paper, doing exactly what Twachtman's tan board does in Connecticut three hundred and sixty years later, except that here it is a settled convention rather than a discovery, and the empty ground has a name and a theory behind it.

Put the two next to each other and the rhyme is almost embarrassing. A Muromachi painter and an American Impressionist arrive at the same solution, that the support should carry the season and the pigment should only mark what departs from it. One got there through a tradition of negative space and the economics of gold leaf, the other by picking up a pastel stick and noticing what happened when he stopped filling the sheet.
The moon rises out of the grass

The other half of the Japanese autumn is not the sun at all. It is the moon. The full moon of the eighth lunar month is the autumn moon, viewed at parties held for the purpose, and the plain called Musashino, west of Edo, is the place-name attached to it: a plain so flat and so thick with susuki that in the poetic formula the moon has nowhere to rise from except the grass itself.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgt0tuvk952y9.jpg
content.caption: Autumn Evening with Full Moon on Musashino Plain, early 1600s. One of a pair of six-fold screens; ink, colour, and gold and silver foil on gilded paper, 170.2 by 346.7 cm. Cleveland Museum of Art, John L. Severance Fund, CC0.

content.content: The screen does what the formula says. A silver moon sits low in a field of miscanthus, and there is no horizon behind it, because the ground it would rise from has been replaced by gold leaf. Measured, the gold band reads plus 99.7 on the same warm-cool scale that gave Cazin's extreme European autumn plus 61. Nothing painted from observation in this article comes close to it.

More telling is the direction of travel inside the picture. The gold at the top is plus 99.7, the grass band across the middle is plus 73.3, and the foreground is plus 25.6. The screen gets cooler as it comes forward, which is the exact inverse of Monet's autumn field, where the ground was the warm end and the sky stayed neutral. In Giverny the warmth had moved down into the stubble because that is what October does to a field. Here the warmth is at the top because the top is metal, and metal is warm regardless of the month.

Two cautions on that number. Gold is a specular surface, so a photograph of it records one particular raking light in one gallery, and the figure describes a warm metallic ground rather than a colorimetric fact. And the silver of the moon has tarnished over four centuries, which is why it now reads as a dark grey disc rather than a bright one. As with the faded pastel papers, the object has aged in a direction that changes the reading: the picture was made with a bright moon and now has a dull one.
Light you can wipe onto a block

In the woodblock print the question of where the light comes from has an unusually literal answer. It comes from the printer's cloth. The graded washes in Hiroshige's skies are bokashi: ink is wiped onto the block by hand in a gradient before each impression, so no two sheets in an edition are identical and the entire atmosphere of a print is a manual gesture performed hundreds of times.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgt0vttzg2e9z.jpg
content.caption: Utagawa Hiroshige. The Moon-Viewing Promontory, from One Hundred Views of Famous Places in Edo, 1857. Colour woodblock print, 33.9 by 22.8 cm. Cleveland Museum of Art, the Kelvin Smith Collection, given by Mrs. Kelvin Smith, CC0.

content.content: Sampled in strips down the sky, the ramp is unmistakably manufactured rather than observed. It runs from a saturated blue at the top, hue 214 with saturation 0.30, through hue 171 at saturation 0.12, to a near-neutral pale at hue 59 and saturation 0.07 by the horizon: one pigment, one wipe, saturation falling smoothly and value rising smoothly. Monet's sky over the stacks does not behave like that. It changes hue as it crosses the canvas, because it was matched to something being looked at.

And the way this sheet says autumn is worth listing, because not one item on the list is a lighting effect. There is a moon, cropped by the eaves so that you register it as a fact rather than a spectacle. There is a line of geese, the standard autumn arrival. There is a room after the party: dishes pushed aside, a lantern, a shadow on the paper screen, the guests gone. The season is a date in the calendar, a bird, a plant and a social occasion, recorded in a print whose light was applied with a rag.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsb3zk5ljp9k.jpg
content.caption: Tosa Mitsuoki. Autumn Maples with Poem Slips, about 1675. Six-panel screen, one of a pair. Ink, colours, gold leaf and gold powder on silk, 144 by 286 cm. Art Institute of Chicago, Kate S. Buckingham Endowment.

content.content: Tosa Mitsuoki's maples close the argument. Measured across the whole surface the screen is 83.5 per cent yellow and ochre, the highest concentration of warm colour anywhere in this set, higher than Cazin, higher than Millet, and yet there is no sun angle in it, no aerial perspective, no cast shadow, nothing that could be called an observation of light. What there is instead is a species, and slips of poetry paper tied to the branches by people who came out to look at the leaves and wrote something down. Momijigari, leaf-hunting, is an outing with a literature attached.

Even the colour vocabulary is codified rather than observed. Traditional Japanese colour names include kuchiba-iro, decayed-leaf colour, a specific brown-yellow with a fixed dye recipe and a fixed place in the wardrobe calendar. A European painter mixes a colour that matches what a leaf is doing this week. A court painter reaches for the colour the season is agreed to have.

Neither system is more accurate. They answer different questions. The European tradition asks what the light is doing right now and builds an instrument, the canvas, sensitive enough to record it. The Japanese tradition asks what season it is according to the calendar and the poems, and then names the plant, the bird and the colour that belong to that answer. The first produces twenty-five wheat stacks in one field. The second produces three and a half metres of a single grass, and a moon with no horizon to rise from.
Where the road ends

The last of the Chicago stacks answers the question the first two open. Measure the snow canvas and the warm bias goes negative, minus 4.3, the only picture in this set whose average is cooler than neutral. Blue and violet take a quarter of the surface. Green is gone to a tenth of one per cent. The orange and red band survives at 15.5 per cent, and almost all of it is inside the stack itself.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtgsb2so4bi36s.jpg
content.caption: Claude Monet. Stack of Wheat, 1890 to 1891. Oil on canvas. Art Institute of Chicago, purchased with funds provided by the Searle Family Trust. The warm mass has retreated into the single made object in the field.

content.content: That is the end of the sequence. The warmth withdraws from the field and concentrates in the one built thing standing in it, and the ground hands the light back to the sky. Autumn is the interval in which that handover is visible, which is why it repays a series rather than a single canvas, and why Monet needed twenty-five of them.
Four questions to take outside

Which is brighter, the sky or the ground. Where is the warmth, in the light or in the shadow. How many planes of distance survive, three or two. And is the yellow spread through the mass while the red arrives in patches, which tells you how far the process has gone. The first two will date a landscape painting to within about six weeks, and they work equally well on the street outside.
Method and sources

Colour figures were computed from open-access reproductions, sampled at reduced resolution, with red-minus-blue used as a warm-cool proxy and pixels grouped into hue families reported as a share of surface. Regional figures come from fixed rectangles in each image, described in the text. These are measurements of photographs, not of paint: museum photography is colour-managed but interpretive, and century-old varnish shifts everything slightly warm. They are meant for comparison between images in the same set. Works from the Art Institute of Chicago, the Cleveland Museum of Art and the Metropolitan Museum of Art appear under their open-access programmes; Levitan's Golden Autumn is in the public domain. Medium and support descriptions, including the records of discoloration, are quoted from the holding institutions' own catalogue entries.

articles.title: The Picture Is Finished Before the Shutter - interview with Roland M Schwerdtfeger
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Roland M Schwerdtfeger
articles.excerpt: Architectural photographer Roland M Schwerdtfeger on planning a picture until it is finished before the camera comes up, the single coloured note in a black-and-white frame, and why camera brand is the wrong question.

content.content: Most architectural photography argues for a building. Roland M Schwerdtfeger's argues past it: a spiral staircase becomes Red Spiral, a bridge becomes pure shape, and the name of the architect who built it stops being the point. Line, shape, light, colour, rhythm – that is the finished list of what survives his edit, and everything else, the function, the address, sometimes even the building's own name, is what gets removed to get there.

He works from research outward. A location is scouted on Google Maps before it is ever visited, checked for orientation and the hour the light will be right, and the picture, he says, is usually finished in his head before the shutter opens at all – the title comes later, sometimes only once the image is published. It is a discipline that has drawn recognition outside his own judgment too: an EPA Platinum Award, an IPA Gold, honours from Fineartphotoawards and ND Awards, and a curator's seat on 1x, the photography platform that has accepted 442 of his images and turned away only three.

Based in Germany, he moves between company premises where a camera is often simply not allowed, museums that grant permission if asked properly, and buildings that sit outside Panoramafreiheit, the country's law protecting only what can be photographed from a public street. What comes home from those visits is edited hard in Lightroom and Photoshop – skies replaced, distractions removed, occasionally a streetlight or a figure added back in – but never, he insists, handed over to AI to compose.

We spoke with Roland about the point where planning ends and the picture takes over, the one colour he lets stand in for all the others, and why – after 442 published images – a camera's brand still tells you less about a photograph than people assume.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqlklceiuxh0.webp
content.caption: Chromatic Encounter, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2026. La Defense, Almere, Netherlands

content.content: 01 · Before the shutter

Viacheslav Munister [VM]: Your titles split in two: some keep their name and stay themselves, like Dreischeibenhaus or Schwebebahn; others lose it and become pure shape, like Red Spiral or Cubic VII. When you raise the camera, do you already know which one this will be?

Roland M Schwerdtfeger [RS]: That's an interesting question. No, when I take a photo, I don't yet know what title it might eventually be published under – once all the post-processing stages are complete. I usually prepare the locations where I take photos very thoroughly. Impressive buildings aren't exactly a dime a dozen, and you first have to find interesting subjects. I often discover my subjects through online research, but also through inspiration from other photographers on 1X, on Instagram, at photography exhibitions and the like.

Then I check Google Maps to determine the location, the surroundings and the orientation of the subject. It's important to choose the right moment to take the shot so that the light is just right. For me, planning and preparation are absolutely essential. My images usually take shape in my mind and are often already 'finished' before I've even taken the photograph. But the title only comes to me when the image is published.
My images usually take shape in my mind and are often already 'finished' before I've even taken the photograph.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqnd7cim5c7s.webp
content.caption: Urban Lines, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2026. Trivago Headquarter, Düsseldorf

content.content: VM: A number implies an unfinished series. What earns a staircase its number rather than leaving it an outtake, and what does a spiral staircase give you that a facade never can?

RS: The number after the name is included because there are often several images with the same name, e.g. 'Staircase' or 'Window Composition'. The number simply serves to distinguish between them; it does not refer to a series. As for the subjects themselves, whilst I remain true to my passion for architectural photography, I am constantly on the lookout for new buildings and details. I am interested in both the subject itself and its effect: lines, shapes, light, colour and rhythm. Sometimes entire buildings, sometimes a staircase, sometimes details of a façade.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqpepeqboquo.webp
content.caption: Staircase, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2026. Glashaus Office building, Krefeld

content.content: 02 · One colour, and where it goes
VM: A viewer on 1x compared your red to Turner's red dot. You thanked him but never said if he was right. Was he, and is there a colour you refuse to let into a frame at all?

RS: He's basically right. The coloured focal point in black-and-white photographs serves a compositional purpose – it draws the eye, provides a counterpoint to large areas of light, sky or landscape, and can thus guide the viewer's gaze. However, it doesn't necessarily have to be a point; colour keys, when used as larger areas, also make many images more attractive. Nor is red the only option. I also like orange, green and blue – depending on the subject. If a building offers no colour at all, a monochrome rendering is often better, although subtle, understated and desaturated colours can also be very attractive.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqp87h3zop02.webp
content.caption: Panta Rhei, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2024. Office building, Düsseldorf

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqpzgmjwque3.webp
content.caption: Contrasts, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. High-rise buildings in Frankfurt/Main

content.content: 03 · The architect's building, the photographer's picture
VM: An architect designs a building to be entered; you show it flat, sometimes as abstraction. Has one ever objected to what you did with their work, or thanked you for it?

RS: There have never been any objections so far. After all, artistic photography is not meant to document, but to abstract and allow aesthetics to take centre stage. Through simplification, perspective and deliberate post-processing, I attempt to remove subjects from their functional context and transform them into an independent world of fine art photography. A good art photograph should not explain, but leave room for interpretation. My images are therefore a conscious, aesthetic and personal interpretation of what I have seen and felt.

For me, photography is much more than just a hobby. It is fulfilment, a philosophy of life, work-life balance and, above all, a passion. It is an essential part of my life. Photography brings me joy. In my view, a good photograph is one that conveys a clear message and appeals to the viewer's emotions. My passion lies in art photography – the artistic aspect, not merely rationality and documentation. For me, post-processing is just as important as the act of taking the photograph itself.

Research is usually the starting point. I only head to the location once I have a clear idea of how I want to capture the subject: the nature of the building, what it looks like, and what the architect intended to express. As for the photos themselves, I usually take plenty of time to choose the right spot, the right angle, the right focal length and so on. However, I usually photograph the subject from various angles, capturing both the overall scene and the finer details. Sometimes the idea for a picture only comes to me afterwards.
A good art photograph should not explain, but leave room for interpretation.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqqqzs9l79rp.webp
content.caption: Looking at the Picture, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Museum of modern art, Münster

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqpw8kp67wpw.webp
content.caption: Neuer Zollhof, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Frank O. Gehry building, Media Harbor, Düsseldorf

content.content: 04 · Asking permission
VM: Germany's Panoramafreiheit covers the street, not an interior like the MAK staircase. What is your actual rule for asking permission, and has it ever cost you a picture?

RS: When I want to take photographs indoors, for example in museums, I ask for permission to do so. This is usually no problem, especially as I generally don't photograph people in a way that makes them recognisable. In public buildings, this is normally no problem either, unlike, for example, in company premises. There, taking photographs indoors is often prohibited. And yes, that has cost me an interesting photo or two on occasion.

However, I've never had any problems so far; if you ask politely, you'll usually get a friendly reply. In the case of religious buildings or specially protected sites, you can also find out about photography permits online in advance and, if necessary, apply for them by email. If in doubt, the rule is: ask politely, point out that the photos are for non-commercial use, and then taking photos is usually no problem.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqqx8n5dvu2s.webp
content.caption: St. Rochus III, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2024. A small church in Düsseldorf

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqqu3k826uwn.webp
content.caption: Natalini Tower, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2024. Traditional building in Roermond, Netherlands

content.content: 05 · After the shutter
VM: How much of an image happens after the shutter closes? Name the line: what would you never remove from a frame, and what goes without a second thought?

RS: It really varies a lot. Every image is edited in Lightroom and Photoshop. Sometimes I only adjust the highlights and shadows, but usually I do more: I replace the sky and remove distracting elements from the image. In some cases, I add elements like streetlights or even people. However, the main subject always remains the most important element and is never removed. I do use AI, but primarily to replace individual elements; it never becomes the designer of the image.
I do use AI, but primarily to replace individual elements; it never becomes the designer of the image.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqp50v9n2ouy.webp
content.caption: Pavilion, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Porsche pavilion, Volkswagen Autostadt, Wolfsburg

content.content: 06 · The jury
VM: 1x refuses most of what it receives; you have 442 accepted. What did the refusals teach you that the acceptances never did, and does a jury change how you edit, honestly?

RS: To be honest, I've only had three rejections so far, which I'm very happy about. As a curator, however, I also see a lot of negative examples and am glad that 1X is such a well-curated platform with very high standards. And no, the jury doesn't change the way I edit my photos; I take and edit photos out of passion, not opportunism. That said, I don't submit any photos that I think wouldn't be accepted. I don't have a single photo on the walls at home. There's only modern art hanging there, no photography.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqpbjeby9vr5.webp
content.caption: A white Cloud, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Museum of modern Art, Münster

content.content: 07 · The print on someone's wall
VM: A print becomes a physical object on someone's wall. What does an image gain in that move, and whom do you picture actually living with it?

RS: A printed photograph, set in a high-quality frame with a passe-partout, becomes an object in its own right and takes on a completely different significance compared to a photograph on a screen. In this way, the image can be elevated to the status of a work of art. By contrast, the screen offers greater brilliance, and the colours are more vibrant. A physical gallery or an exhibition opening conveys a very different atmosphere to an online gallery; the impression and the experience are entirely different. And both have their place.

Who do I picture with photos on the wall? This is certainly more than one target audience; when it comes to architectural photos, perhaps people with modern, contemporary interiors rather than traditionalists. Design enthusiasts rather than nostalgics. Yes, it has happened that photos have impressed me on screen, only to disappoint when seen as prints. The size of the print also sometimes plays a role. There are photos that have a greater impact as their size increases. Weak photos, on the other hand, do not improve with a large format…
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqq8wkgzubn1.webp
content.caption: Sluishuis, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Apartment building near Amsterdam, Netherlands

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqq5t7g2zyfw.webp
content.caption: Zaandam Facades, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Composition of buildings in Zaandam, North Holland

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqq2o4hgertf.webp
content.caption: Zaandam V, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. Hotel in Zaandam, North Holland

content.content: 08 · Two he would take back
VM: Of 442 published images, is there one you'd take back, and what question about your work are you tired of being asked, that nobody else asks instead?

RS: Yes, there are indeed two photos that I wouldn't publish today; unfortunately, you can't delete them on 1X… I'm always happy to answer questions, and I never tire of them. Sometimes, though, I hear people say: 'Your photos are brilliant – what camera do you use?' That always makes me smile. Of course, you need a system camera and the right kit; there are lots of things you simply can't achieve with just a standard lens. But ultimately, the brand of camera doesn't matter. You can't tell from a photo which camera was used to take it.
You can't tell from a photo which camera was used to take it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtjqqnxivdjz2h.webp
content.caption: Portikus, Roland M Schwerdtfeger, 2025. A small museum in Frankfurt/Main

content.content: Roland M Schwerdtfeger's work can be seen at 1x.com/rolandmschwerdtfeger and on Instagram at @roland_m_schwerdtfeger. All images © Roland M Schwerdtfeger, published with the artist's permission.

articles.title: Neobarocco: Five Buildings That Confess What They Want You to Believe
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: No seventeenth-century architect ever had to build a case for absolute power. The power was already absolute, and the architecture only had to make it beautiful. Today's patrons aren't so lucky. A state that isn't sure of its own legitimacy, a brand selling heritage it never had, a city that needs the world to stop laughing at it: each has hired a very different architect to do Bernini's old job. Five buildings, five confessions.

content.content: Nobody in Hamburg asked for the Elbphilharmonie to be beautiful. For most of a decade they asked, loudly and in print, for it to stop. A concert hall budgeted in 2001 at €77 million and meant to open in 2010 crept to €114 million by 2005, to €241 million when the schedule slipped again in 2007, past €450 million after the construction contract was renegotiated in 2008, past €500 million by 2012, and finally opened in January 2017 at a confirmed €866 million, on top of a squat 1960s brick warehouse that had spent those same years gutted down to its four outer walls while the number kept climbing. Herzog & de Meuron's answer to a decade of civic fury was not an apology. It was a curved glass crown, faceted like sea ice, that catches the harbor and the sky in whatever light happens to be passing, and does the one thing an over-budget public building is never supposed to manage. It makes the argument about the money evaporate the moment you actually look at it. Within a year, the same city that had wanted somebody fired was posting sunset photographs of the thing.

That is not resilience. That is a very old trick, running on new material, and it worked exactly as designed. A building that makes you feel something is true before you have had time to ask whether it was a good idea: Bernini would have recognized the move on sight, and would not have been remotely surprised that it worked twice.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1ry50b1aw12.jpg
content.alt: Visitors ascending the long curved escalator tube inside the Elbphilharmonie toward the Grand Hall
content.caption: Inside the Elbphilharmonie: the curved escalator tube rising toward the Großer Saal.
content.credit: Photo: Arths-at / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: What the word meant before it became a compliment

“Baroque” gets thrown around now as a synonym for ornate, curved, expensive: an adjective for a feeling, not a claim about how a building actually works. The historical style was a great deal more specific, and a great deal more useful as a lens than the loose modern usage suggests.

Take the single clearest demonstration of it: Bernini's Cornaro Chapel in Santa Maria della Vittoria, finished in 1652. At its center, the marble Ecstasy of Saint Teresa shows the saint mid-vision, an angel about to drive a golden arrow through her, her whole body gone slack with a pain she described as indistinguishable from the love of God. Bernini did not simply carve a sculpture and set it in a niche. He cut a hidden window into the wall above the group and ran gilded bronze rods down through the marble like frozen sunlight, so that real daylight and sculpted light arrive at the same figure at once. On either side, members of the Cornaro family are carved leaning out of what are unmistakably theater boxes, watching the ecstasy the way an audience watches a stage. Architecture, sculpture, hidden engineering and stage lighting are fused into a single continuous event with no seam anywhere between the craft and the persuasion. Art historians have a term for exactly this ambition, bel composto, the beautiful whole, and it describes something considerably more disciplined than “ornate.”

So the useful question about anything called neo-baroque today has nothing to do with curves. It is: who commissioned the disappearing act, and what exactly were they hoping the audience would feel before it had the chance to examine the argument underneath.
Zaha Hadid, Baku: the argument is the country
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1ryrutoiold.jpg
content.alt: The Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, its white curved form rising continuously from the plaza
content.caption: Heydar Aliyev Center, Baku. Zaha Hadid Architects with Werner Sobek, 2012.
content.credit: Photo: Robot8A / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: The Heydar Aliyev Center has no facade, no roofline, no wall in the ordinary sense: plaza and building are one continuous white skin, roughly 39,100 square meters of it plus another 9,000 of plaza, that lifts off the ground, folds through the interior and lies back down on the far side. Werner Sobek's office engineered the whole envelope from around 15,000 individually curved fiber-reinforced panels, no two alike, some as long as seven meters, without a single straight structural line doing the actual work of holding the thing up. Zaha Hadid built it in open opposition to the Soviet concrete still standing across Baku: block after honest, humorless block asserting permanence through mass. The Center asserts the opposite: a young petrostate telling the world, in one unbroken gesture, that it has moved on. The Architectural Review's verdict on first contact was that the building is “a shock to the system,” which is precisely the effect a persuasive building is built to produce.

The Center was originally budgeted at around $250 million for 57,500 square meters, a number that still puts it among the most expensive buildings ever raised per square foot, on a site cleared, according to Human Rights Watch, by force: roughly 250 homes removed to make room for the gesture. Put those two facts beside the white curve in any photograph and the building stops reading as architecture and starts reading as what it actually is: a receipt for how much a country will spend, and who it will move, to make sure the world watches it curve instead of asking why.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1rz1c52q7fy.jpg
content.alt: An orchestra performing inside the concert hall of the Heydar Aliyev Center, its curved wooden walls wrapping the stage
content.caption: Inside the Center: the same unbroken curve continues into the concert hall.
content.credit: Photo: Eminn / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: Calatrava, Valencia: the skeleton performing innocence
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1rzbnkh313h.jpg
content.alt: The City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia, white ribbed structures over reflecting pools
content.caption: City of Arts and Sciences, Valencia. Santiago Calatrava, 1998–2005.
content.credit: Photo: Cateecatee / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

content.content: Nothing in the City of Arts and Sciences needs to look the way it looks. A planetarium does not require ribs. A science museum does not need to resemble the picked-clean skeleton of a whale, which is exactly what Calatrava's Museu de les Ciències resembles, on purpose, across two kilometers of Valencia's drained Turia riverbed. This is engineering doing a painted ceiling's job: performing an illusion of structural necessity where there was only choice, the same way Baroque fresco performs a hole in a flat surface opening onto open sky.

It is gorgeous. It is also, in the most literal sense, a magic trick that started coming apart. A complex estimated at roughly €300 million landed near €1.1 billion, with Calatrava's own fees for the project alleged at around €100 million on top, a pattern repeating itself closely enough across his career, from Valencia to Venice to a transit hub built over the ruins of the World Trade Center, that the press settled on calling him “the world's most hated architect.” In 2013, ceramic tiles began detaching from the roof and mosaic facade of the Palau de les Arts opera house at the complex's center; by mid-2014 the regional government had filed suit against Calatrava's firm over the defects. The skeleton, it turned out, was shedding its skin. Someone always pays extra for the sky to look this open: first in the invoice, and later, it seems, in the roof.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1rzn2676c54.jpg
content.alt: A sculptural white spiral staircase inside the Palau de les Arts, cantilevered under a curved concrete ceiling
content.caption: Inside the Palau de les Arts: the same structural drama, indoors and unpainted.
content.credit: Photo: Kippelboy / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

content.content: Neo-baroque architecture is not a style. It is what a client pays for when the truth alone will not get the reaction they need.
Ma Yansong, Harbin: the one building here that owes Rome nothing
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1rzxi9wupf2.jpg
content.alt: The Harbin Opera House, its sweeping white aluminum form set against the wetlands
content.caption: Harbin Opera House. MAD Architects (Ma Yansong), 2015.
content.credit: Photo: EditQ / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: Every essay like this one risks smuggling in an unstated assumption: that the appetite for movement and illusion under discussion is a European inheritance, waiting somewhere to be exported. The Harbin Opera House refuses the premise outright. Ma Yansong has described the building as shaped by wind and water rather than by any Italian precedent: white aluminum panels sweeping across the wetlands beside the Songhua River on the outside, a warm, wind-eroded mass of Manchurian ash inside the main hall, the whole thing closer to a mountain range dissolving into mist in a Song dynasty scroll than to anything Bernini ever touched. MAD won the international competition for the surrounding Harbin Cultural Island in 2010; the opera house itself, roughly 850,000 square feet of it, opened in December 2015 to a city better known internationally, until then, for winter ice sculpture festivals than for architecture.

It belongs in this company anyway, and that is the point worth sitting with. The instinct this essay is tracking, fuse a building into one continuous sensation, argue through the body before the mind gets a vote, is not a Roman export. It surfaces wherever an architect has the tools, a client willing to fund wonder rather than only shelter, and a visual tradition of their own to spend that funding on. Harbin owes the Vatican nothing. It still speaks the same underlying language, fluently, in an accent entirely its own.
Peter Marino: the one who stopped pretending

Hadid, Calatrava and Ma each arrive at a Baroque effect by other means and other materials, translating the seventeenth century's tools of persuasion into fiberglass, structural steel, aluminum. Peter Marino skips the translation and imports the source text directly. Since the early 1980s his flagship stores for Chanel and Dior have set genuine eighteenth-century bronzes and actual Venetian mirrors against blunt, contemporary architectural shells, on purpose, and by his own account with some relish: he has spoken about how rarely anyone dares put something fully modern next to something fully Baroque, and about the collision being the entire exercise, not an accident of taste. The 2004 Chanel tower in Tokyo's Ginza district takes the house's signature black-and-white tweed and detonates it across an entire glazed facade at architectural scale. The reworked Dior flagship on Avenue Montaigne in Paris wraps the boutique itself in a two-thousand-square-meter museum and three private gardens, in case the point somehow wasn't landing already.

This is the case that makes the essay's real question impossible to keep dodging politely. A handbag does not require eighteenth-century provenance to function as a handbag. The bronzes and the mirrors are there to argue, silently and at considerable expense, that the object for sale is heir to a grandeur the brand behind it did not actually inherit: it purchased the props and installed them under gallery lighting, the way a museum installs a period room. Marino is the only architect in this set who is not hiding that this is what he is doing. Whether that honesty is the most respectable thing about his work, or the most cynical, does not seem like a question with room for a third answer.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mto1s0al7n32z0.jpg
content.alt: The Dior flagship at 30 Avenue Montaigne, Paris, its Haussmannian facade lit with an oversized illuminated chandelier installation
content.caption: 30 Avenue Montaigne, Paris, 2016, before Marino's 2022 renovation, the same address already staging its own excess directly on the street.
content.credit: Photo: Frédéric BISSON / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0

content.content: Where the word stops being useful

Not everything curved and expensive has earned the comparison, and it is worth refusing the lazy version of it on principle. A building deserves “neo-baroque” when its movement and illusion are doing real rhetorical work: arguing for a state's legitimacy, or a brand's inherited weight, or a city's right to stop being laughed at. A building that simply runs parametric software to arrive at an unusual silhouette, with nothing riding on the shape beyond novelty, is not neo-baroque. It is just curved, and calling it baroque performs the same flattening the word already suffers everywhere from real-estate listings to Instagram captions.

What earns these five their place is not a family resemblance of surface. It is that each is trying to make a viewer feel an argument before they have had the chance to interrogate it, in the exact visual grammar the seventeenth century invented for that specific purpose, which three and a half centuries of intervening architecture mostly tried, and largely failed, to argue its way out of.

Bernini never had to build a case for the Pope's authority. The authority was already absolute; the architecture only had to make it beautiful. Nobody commissioning a building today has that luxury, which is exactly why digital fabrication's cheap, borrowed freedom of form keeps ending up in the hands of clients who need an audience feeling something before it starts asking questions: a state without a settled story about itself, a brand selling a history it bought rather than lived, a city that would rather be photographed than interrogated. The style survived the collapse of absolute power by outliving the thing it was built to defend. What is left standing is the technique, and the technique, it turns out, does not need to believe in anything at all in order to work.

articles.title: Built to a Score: Three Buildings Where Music Wrote the Architecture
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Most buildings host music: a stage, walls, a program, good acoustics. A handful of buildings do something stranger, and let a piece of music design them outright, or let the problem of holding sound decide everything from the roof down to the seats. Three buildings, three different bargains between the two disciplines.

content.content: In 1958, Le Corbusier's studio built a pavilion for Philips at the Brussels World's Fair that had no straight walls at all: nine curved concrete shells, tent-like and pointed, standing over a single dark hall built for eight minutes of music. The shape did not come from a sketch of a building. It came from a piece of music.

The shells were the work of Iannis Xenakis, a composer working as an engineer in Le Corbusier's atelier, and their geometry traces back to his orchestral piece Metastaseis (1953-54). Xenakis had scored a passage for forty-six string instruments sliding continuously between pitches, glissando lines drawn as straight lines on paper that, taken together, described curved surfaces: what a mathematician would call a ruled surface, and what an engineer would recognise as a hyperbolic paraboloid. Xenakis modelled the pavilion's walls the same way he had modelled the glissandi, string and stiff wire standing in for sound. The building is, in a fairly literal sense, a piece of music built at architectural scale.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsjcy0zh4fu43.jpg
content.caption: The Philips Pavilion at Expo 58, Brussels: nine concrete shells, each one a ruled surface of the kind Xenakis had drawn as glissandi. Photo: Anefo, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.content: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jjpq2Y4tUGI
content.caption: Iannis Xenakis, Metastaseis (1953-54), for 61 musicians. The glissandi behind the pavilion's shells.

content.content: Inside, some 350 loudspeakers set into those walls spatialised Edgard Varèse's Poème électronique, an eight-minute tape piece routed live around the audience by technicians at a control desk, timed to shifts of coloured light. The pavilion was demolished on 30 January 1959, three months after the fair closed, its purpose used up with the event that paid for it. What survives is the method: music read not as a soundtrack for a room, but as a set of instructions for building one.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MmrchX7qYpU
content.caption: Edgard Varèse, Poème électronique (1958). Composed for the Philips Pavilion's 350 loudspeakers.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsjcyljd4lptv.jpg
content.caption: Elbphilharmonie, Hamburg: the glass upper storeys, each pane curved or cut, sitting directly on the brick of the Kaispeicher warehouse. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.credit: Photo: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Nearly sixty years later, Herzog & de Meuron's Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg, opened 11 January 2017, made the opposite bargain: instead of letting music generate the building's form, it let the requirements of hearing music decide almost everything else. Acoustician Yasuhisa Toyota laid the main hall out as a vineyard, terraces of seating climbing around a central stage in the manner Hans Scharoun had used for the Berlin Philharmonie in 1963, so that no listener among 2,100 sits more than 30 metres from the conductor. The hall's inner surface, some 10,000 individually milled gypsum-fibre panels, is cut with a different profile at every point to scatter sound evenly rather than let it collect in one place. The whole structure floats on 362 spring bearings, mechanically isolated from the building around it so that a passing train never reaches the stage. Above a converted brick warehouse, the concert hall's glass upper storeys read from outside as a wave, or a crown. From inside the hall, that image is almost beside the point: the room's actual job is acoustic, and its shape is a diagram of that job.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsjczm6llszor.jpg
content.caption: Casa da Música, Porto: one of the folded concrete planes, with the corrugated glass that lights the hall behind it. Photo: Dale Cruse, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
content.credit: Photo: John Samuel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: Rem Koolhaas and Ellen van Loon's OMA took a third position with Casa da Música in Porto, opened in 2005. The office wanted to avoid the concert hall's standard shoebox shape, tried alternatives, and measured them against the shoebox on acoustics it could not beat. So OMA kept the box and hid it: a rectangular hall seating around 1,200, glazed at both ends, sits inside an irregular white polyhedron that looks folded rather than built, as if the shoebox had been quarried out of a single asymmetric block. The shape the building wears on the outside has no obvious logic until you know there is a straight, acoustically correct room sitting inside it, and that everything faceted and irregular on the exterior is the architecture finding a public form for a decision it was not free to make.

Three buildings, three different relationships to the same problem. Xenakis let a piece of music become a roof. Toyota and Herzog & de Meuron let the physics of hearing dictate a room, then wrapped a building around the result. Koolhaas kept the one shape acoustics insists on and spent the rest of the building arguing with it. None of the three is really about music in architecture. They are about what happens when a discipline that runs on sequence and proportion is allowed to give orders to one that runs on load and material, or is made to answer to it instead.

Photographs: cover, Elbphilharmonie on its opening night, 11 January 2017, Alexander Svensson (CC BY 2.0); Philips Pavilion, Anefo (CC0); Elbphilharmonie facade, Dietmar Rabich (CC BY-SA 4.0); Casa da Música, Dale Cruse (CC BY 4.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: The Seam That Isn't There: Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate has no front, no seam and, its maker insists, no fixed subject beyond the skyline and the crowd currently caught in its surface. On the engineering problem that took two extra years and $23 million to solve, the omphalos underneath that turns the trick on the viewer, and why the solution still works two decades on.

content.content: Cloud Gate has no front. Walk Millennium Park from any direction and the sculpture that Chicago calls the Bean turns to meet you: a continuous, gateless loop of polished steel, 20 metres long and 13 metres wide, sitting on the Michigan Avenue lawn like a drop of mercury caught mid-fall before it can spread. The city's public art program asked, in 1999, for a landmark for a new plaza on top of a rail yard. What it received, after a jury reviewed an international shortlist and Anish Kapoor's design was chosen over more conventional proposals, was his first permanent outdoor work built in the United States, and a piece of sculpture whose entire content is the city looking at itself, bent.
A surface with no seam to hide behind

The engineering problem was the whole project. Kapoor's design called for a mirror-polished skin with no visible joints anywhere on its surface, which meant 168 stainless steel plates had to be welded edge to edge and then ground and buffed by hand until the welds disappeared entirely. There is no trim, no gasket, no seam moulding to break the reflection and remind a viewer that the object in front of them was assembled rather than poured. Underneath that skin sits an independent steel frame engineered to breathe with Chicago's weather: the whole structure grows and shrinks by several centimetres between a July heat wave and a January cold snap, and the polished plates have to move with it without ever telegraphing a crease to the surface. Reaching that standard took two years longer than scheduled. Millennium Park opened in 2004; Cloud Gate, still hidden behind construction fencing, opened to the public in 2006, and the roughly $23 million the sculpture and its plaza eventually cost ran well past the original estimate, almost entirely on account of the polishing.

That decision is the piece's real subject. A seamed surface reads as construction: an object built by people, in time, out of parts. A seamless one reads as a phenomenon, less a sculpture of something than a hole cut in the world where a 110-tonne solid ought to be, through which the sky, the Aon Center and several thousand tourists a day pour continuously. Kapoor had spent much of the previous two decades chasing this effect at gallery scale, in the pigment-filled voids of the 1980s and the concave mirrored discs that followed, works where the viewer's own reflection curls back distorted rather than sitting flat on a surface. Cloud Gate is the moment that vocabulary met a civic budget and a skyline large enough to be worth swallowing, and it set the pattern for the mirrored public commissions Kapoor would go on to build elsewhere: Sky Mirror in London and New York, the C-Curve at Kensington Gardens, Turning the World Upside Down in Jerusalem. None of the later pieces attempt the same trick at the same scale.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtrhfed6qreyhx.jpg
content.caption: Sky Mirror (for Hendrik), 2017, at Museum de Pont, Tilburg: one of several later Kapoor mirror commissions that work at a fraction of Cloud Gate's scale and budget, and none aim for its seamless, walk-around continuity.
content.credit: Photo: Peter Cox, courtesy Museum De Pont, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtrgodyquzi3fq.jpg
content.caption: Cloud Gate against the Michigan Avenue skyline, on AT&T Plaza. The kidney-bean profile that gave the sculpture its nickname, never Kapoor's own name for it, is legible only from outside; the work itself has no single correct viewing angle.

content.content: Underneath, the plates curve inward to form what the artist calls the omphalos, an eight-metre concave chamber that gathers the reflections back on themselves and multiplies them into a compressed, curling vortex of tile, sky and crowd. It is the one part of the sculpture where the mirror stops behaving politely. Everywhere else, Cloud Gate flatters its surroundings, stretching the skyline into something taller and stranger than it actually is. Under the arch, the same surface turns on the viewer instead, folding dozens of people into a single circular frame with no horizon and no fixed vantage point to stand at and call correct.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtrh4o4bclo49h.jpg
content.caption: Looking straight up into the omphalos: the concave underside compresses the plaza, the crowd and the sky into a single continuous ring with no horizon.

content.content: Public sculpture as infrastructure

What makes Cloud Gate an unusually successful piece of public art, rather than merely a popular one, is how little it asks of anyone who did not come to look at sculpture. It has no plaque-length argument to absorb, no fixed reading distance, no correct time of day. A tourist photographing their own reflection and a critic tracing Kapoor's debt to Brancusi's polished bronzes and to the biomorphic abstraction of Jean Arp are using the same object for the same reason: because its surface changes with whoever is standing in front of it and never resolves into one fixed image to be checked off and left. That is a harder trick to engineer than the seamless steel. Most large civic commissions settle for legibility from a bus window; this one was built to reward the two minutes someone spends walking around it far more than the two seconds someone spends driving past, which is also why it survives being photographed several million times a year without wearing out as an experience the way a static monument would.

Two decades on, the sculpture has absorbed a nickname it was never given by its maker, appeared in more amateur photographs than almost any other work of contemporary art, and remained, underneath all of that circulation, a genuinely difficult object: a solid with the visual behaviour of a liquid, a monument with no fixed subject except the crowd currently caught in its surface. Cloud Gate did not need an anniversary or a retrospective to prove the seamless finish was worth the extra two years and the extra cost. Every clear afternoon in the plaza does that instead.

articles.title: Abbie Downey: Collected, Not Coordinated
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Abbie Downey
articles.excerpt: The founder of Feather&Fossil on visual rhythm, the difference between layered and chaotic, and why a home should read as continued rather than preserved.

content.content: EPRIS Journal's interview series turns this month to Abbie Downey, founder of the Devon studio Feather&Fossil and one of the designers embracing the return of colour and pattern in British interiors after a long stretch of restraint. Her rooms are dense, layered and unmistakably lived-in – which is where our conversation begins.

She is renovating a Georgian house, her second period property, and that is a useful thing to know before looking at her rooms. Feather&Fossil deals in painted stripes and blue fireplaces, figured wallpaper above blue patterned tile, a wall of framed prints and mirrors hung close. It reads as abundance. It is, on closer inspection, a set of decisions.

Recognised through Next in Design, Downey belongs to a generation of British designers rehabilitating pattern and colour after years in which restraint was treated as the only adult position. Her argument is not that more is better. It is that a room should be able to hold the people who live in it, including the parts of them that do not photograph neatly. We sent her seven questions.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsirxbwsvcgzu.png
content.caption: A sitting room by Feather&Fossil: hand-painted stripes, a fireplace in soft blue, and a cabinet holding a family’s collections rather than a display.

content.content: Your interiors are expressive, but they never feel accidental. When you build up layers of colour, pattern and objects, what tells you that they belong together rather than simply competing for attention?

I think the difference between a room that feels layered and one that feels chaotic is usually intention. For me, maximalism isn’t about simply putting more things into a room; it’s about creating relationships between them. Colour, pattern, texture and objects can all be quite bold individually, but there needs to be something that connects them, a commonality. This could be a repeated colour, a shared undertone, a shape or material that appears more than once.

I also believe there is an element of instinct to bringing maximalist schemes together. We shouldn’t feel afraid of elements competing for attention because I personally quite like a room that gives you something new to notice each time you look at it. But there needs to be a visual rhythm to it. I tend to stand back and look at the room as a whole rather than judging every element individually. There need to be elements of loud and quiet, light and shade, to allow a room to feel cohesive and successful.

Ultimately, I want a room to feel collected rather than coordinated. I’m much more interested in creating a sense that things have found their way together over time than making everything look like it came from the same collection.
When you begin a room, what tends to pull everything else into place? Is it usually one object, a colour, a fabric, or is it more of a gut feeling at the start?

For me, there isn’t really one formula, which is probably why I find the process so enjoyable. Sometimes it’s one element that starts everything: a piece of fabric, a piece of art, a vintage find. Sometimes it’s a client’s must-have piece that starts the process, and often it will be centred around essentials such as the room layout or the practicalities of modern family life.

Quite often, though, it’s a feeling. I’ll have an instinct about the direction I want to take something before I can necessarily articulate exactly why. I think that comes from constantly absorbing interiors, architecture, travel, art and the world around me. You build up this visual library without necessarily realising it, and eventually you start making connections almost instinctively.

I also like to let a room evolve rather than trying to decide everything at once. I might know the colour palette and have one or two key pieces, but I want there to be room for the unexpected. Some of my favourite elements are the things that weren’t necessarily part of the original plan.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsirtd5vrdsml.jpg
content.caption: The kitchen: figured wallpaper above blue patterned tile, with brass taps over a metal sink. Pattern is allowed to sit against pattern.

content.content: Older homes carry traces of the lives that came before us, in the architecture, the materials, the alterations, even the small imperfections. How much do you try to uncover that history before making new decisions, and do you see your role as preserving the story or continuing it?

I think older homes tell you a lot if you’re willing to listen to them. I’m particularly drawn to Georgian, Victorian and Edwardian properties because they have a sense of identity before you’ve even put anything in them. The proportions, fireplaces, floors, mouldings and little imperfections all contribute to that.

I’m interested in understanding a building’s history, but I don’t think that means trying to turn it into a museum. Homes are meant to evolve. There will always be layers of different lives within them, and I think the most successful interiors acknowledge those layers rather than trying to erase them or preserve them to the point that it becomes impractical for modern family life.

That’s something I’ve become particularly conscious of through renovating my own Georgian home. You start noticing all the evidence of the people who have lived there before you: the changes they made, the things they repaired, the things that have survived through good craftsmanship. I find that incredibly interesting.
So I’d say my role is less about preserving a story exactly as it was and more about continuing it. I want new interventions to feel like they belong in the conversation with what was already there.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsirn5pg44cw9.jpg
content.caption: A worn tabletop and a woven runner, photographed close: a surface that records use rather than conceals it.

content.content: The domestic interior has always been a form of self-representation, shaped by taste, memory and the objects people choose to live with. Do you see a home almost as a personal archive, and how do you translate something that private into a room?
Absolutely. The best homes, to me, are the ones where you can learn something about the people who live there simply by looking around.

I think our homes contain so much more of us than we sometimes realise. The objects we keep, the colours we gravitate towards, the things we inherit, the places we’ve travelled to and even the things we refuse to get rid of all tell a story.

That’s one of the reasons I love working with clients. I’m not interested in imposing a particular version of what I think their home should look like. I want to understand what makes them feel at home. Sometimes that comes through in obvious ways (a collection, a piece of furniture or something with sentimental value), and sometimes it’s much more subtle.

I see the design process as a kind of translation. A client might know that they want their home to feel warm, joyful, grown-up or slightly eccentric without knowing exactly how to achieve that visually. My job is to take those very personal, sometimes quite intangible things and turn them into colour, pattern, texture, furniture and objects.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsiry9sr2frcb.jpg
content.caption: The gallery wall. Prints, mirrors, postcards and a Vogue cover, hung against painted stripes.

content.content: Maximalism has long existed in tension with restraint, order and the idea of “good taste”. Do you see contemporary maximalism partly as a reaction against those hierarchies?

I think there has been a long-standing idea that good taste means knowing when to stop: that restraint, simplicity and minimalism are somehow more sophisticated. Maximalism challenges that idea because it allows people to enjoy things simply because they love them.

I don’t think that means minimalism is wrong, or that every room needs to be filled with pattern and colour. It’s more about questioning the idea that there is one correct way for a home to look. Why shouldn’t a room be joyful? Why shouldn’t you display a slightly ridiculous collection simply because it makes you happy?

That freedom is a big part of what attracted me to maximalism. I love colour, pattern, vintage pieces, things with history and interiors that have a little bit of eccentricity to them. I’m much more interested in whether something feels meaningful than whether it fits neatly into an accepted definition of good taste.

For me, contemporary maximalism isn’t really about rebellion for the sake of it. It’s about giving people permission to trust their own instincts and to live in a space that represents them, feels like home and embraces who they are.
I want a room to feel collected rather than coordinated.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsirrrfz5p0nu.jpg
content.caption: A sunburst panel over the fireplace, framed by wallpaper that refuses to recede. Nothing here is trying to be quiet.

content.content: Our sense of taste often comes from things we absorb almost without noticing: the homes we grew up in, places we visit, family objects. What do you think has shaped your own visual taste the most?

Probably a combination of places, buildings and the things I’ve collected along the way. I’ve always been drawn to older buildings and interiors with a sense of history, and I love the way colour and pattern are used in places like Morocco, Mexico, Spain and Italy. There’s something about those spaces that feels incredibly instinctive: pattern sitting alongside pattern, strong colour, texture, craftsmanship and objects with a sense of age.

I’m also very influenced by the idea of things being collected rather than perfectly matched. Vintage and reclaimed pieces have always appealed to me because they bring a sense of history and individuality that you simply can’t get from buying everything at once.

And then there are the homes I’ve lived in. Throughout my childhood, my dad would constantly be reinventing our home and rooms. He was never constrained by the style of house we lived in, but was led more by what he loved: crafting, making and experimenting. Then, living in rented, minimal new-builds through my twenties made me yearn for a home that was full of character, personality and history. This led me to renovate my first home and now my second. Both are period properties, and both have been approached with a maximalist mindset that celebrates our style as a family: the things we love, little moments of joy in everyday life, and a home that feels designed to be lived in, not just to look good in a photograph.

I think a lot of our visual taste develops almost unconsciously. You absorb things from childhood, travel, books, films, buildings, people and places, and eventually all those little influences start to emerge in your own work.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsis1c266ocsm.jpg
content.caption: A rattan chair in a small room papered floor to ceiling, with a second papered room beyond it.

content.content: Being recognised through Next in Design has brought your work into a much wider conversation. As your practice grows, is there anything about the way you work that you feel especially determined to protect?
Probably the freedom to follow my instincts.

Being recognised through Next in Design has been such an exciting moment for Feather&Fossil and has opened the door to opportunities I could never have imagined when I started. It’s incredibly validating.

But I don’t want growth to make the work feel less personal. I want to keep that sense of curiosity and playfulness, and I want to continue designing spaces that have personality rather than simply following whatever happens to be considered fashionable.

I also want to protect the belief that a home should feel like the people who live there. I don’t want to create interiors that are perfect but interchangeable. I want to keep championing colour, pattern, vintage pieces, individuality and the slightly unexpected.

If anything, being recognised through Next in Design has given me more confidence to trust that instinct rather than less. I think the thing I’m most determined to protect is that feeling of freedom: the freedom to experiment, to be a little bit bold, and to make decisions because they feel right rather than seeking approval from others.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtsis04peqgigs.jpg
content.caption: A working corner: an antique desk, a red glass-fronted cabinet, hanging jute baskets.
Feather&Fossil, details.
alts: A brass pendant and a sunburst panel above a papered chimney breast.
Brass taps against blue patterned tile.
A mantelpiece with a painted mirror, two patterned vessels and a lamp with a green shade.

articles.title: Eighteen Inches of Sky: The Interiors of the World Trade Center
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: Twenty five years on, the towers are remembered as a silhouette. Inside they were three buildings stacked on each other, a lobby seventy four feet high, an office floor of nearly an acre, and a window eighteen inches wide that decided how the city was allowed to be looked at.

content.content: Everyone knows the outline. Two flat topped verticals, aluminium turning pink at the end of an afternoon, printed on more posters than any other pair of buildings in the world. What almost nobody describes, twenty five years on, is what it was like to be inside them. About fifty thousand people worked in the World Trade Center on an ordinary day and tens of thousands more passed through it. Their subject was never the silhouette. It was a lobby, an elevator transfer, a floor of grey carpet where the view arrived in slices.
01Eighteen inches

Start with the window, because the rest of the interior follows from it. Minoru Yamasaki wrapped the towers in closely spaced steel columns, and the glass between them is eighteen inches wide, narrower than the shoulders of the person looking through it. The stated reason is disarmingly personal. Yamasaki was afraid of heights, and he did not think a tenant should be asked to stand at a sheer wall of glass a thousand feet in the air. The structural reason ran alongside it, since those same columns were holding the building up.

From inside, the effect is precise and strange. You cannot take in the room and the view at the same time. The city arrives in vertical strips, edited by aluminium. To look down you have to walk right up to the glass and put your face into the opening, and the column takes your weight while you do it. The building makes you commit to looking.

There was one exception, and it proves the rule. On the observation deck near the top of the South Tower the columns were narrowed so the glass could open to twenty eight inches. Ten inches is the entire difference between a place where people work and a place where people come to look.

The deck was a designed attraction rather than a window someone happened to leave open. Top of the World, as the Port Authority called it, opened in December 1975 with an indoor floor at the hundred and seventh level and an open roof deck above it, reached by escalator. It held two dozen video monitors, a film called Manhattan Magic, a model of the city with seven hundred and fifty buildings in it, and a food court with a Sbarro and a Nathan's Famous. A visitor was sold the view in the way a museum sells a collection, with an interpretation attached.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvi6y32h5uqwm.jpg
content.caption: The open deck on the roof of the South Tower in 1984, with the North Tower and its mast beyond. Here the parapet is chest high and the view is the point.
content.credit: Photo: Lars Plougmann, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvi6yu5yjoer3.jpg
content.caption: Coin telescopes and a queue for them. Two floors below, the same building gave its office tenants eighteen inches of glass and no railing to lean on.
content.credit: Photo: Tequask, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: 02A nave at the door

At the bottom the same columns do something else entirely. Near the ground each group of three merges into one, which let the lobby glass run wide and tall between them and let the elevator shafts stack economically above. The lobbies were seventy four feet high. The effect was a pointed arcade, and critics reached for the word Gothic, sometimes admiringly and often not. What matters for the interior is the sequence. The building narrows the world to eighteen inches upstairs and greets you with something like a nave at the door.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvhptzo49xs0a.jpg
content.caption: Where three perimeter columns merge into one, the wall opens. Fritz Koenig's bronze Sphere stands in the plaza fountain beyond.
content.credit: Photo: Balthazar Korab, public domain, via the Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons

content.content: 03Three buildings, stacked

Inside, each tower was not one building but three sitting on top of one another. Floors one to forty three, forty four to seventy seven, seventy eight to one hundred and ten: three zones, each with its own local elevators, reached by express cars running to sky lobbies on the forty fourth and seventy eighth floors. The express cars carried fifty five people at sixteen hundred feet a minute, roughly twenty seven feet every second.

This was arithmetic before it was architecture. In a conventional scheme a tower of this height spends its lower floors on elevator shafts and the rentable area collapses. Splitting the journey the way a subway line splits into express and local raised usable floor area from sixty two to seventy five percent. Thirteen percent of a hundred and ten floors is a great deal of building. The consequence was social. A sky lobby behaved like a station: people changed there, queued there, ran into each other there, and the tower acquired two interior addresses that were neither the street nor an office.

Eight of the hundred and ten floors were never let to anyone. They went to machinery, in four two floor bands spaced up the building, because a tower this size is a utility company that happens to have tenants: its own water, its own air, its own power distribution, its own drainage lifted back down. The complex even had postcodes of its own, 10048 and 10047, which is the plainest possible statement of what it was. Not a building on a street, a settlement with an address.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvhpuu00mgxnj.jpg
content.caption: A tower lobby under construction in 1971. Two years later the same volume held stone, glass and a queue for the express elevators.
content.credit: Photo: Warren K. Leffler, U.S. News & World Report collection, public domain, via the Library of Congress

content.content: 04An acre of ordinary

The floors themselves were plain and enormous. Each plate is a square of two hundred and eight feet with a service core of eighty seven by one hundred and thirty five in the middle, and the ring of space between core and facade runs uninterrupted, which was the whole commercial argument: close to an acre a floor with nothing in the way. What tenants did with that was what tenants do. Partitions, carpet tile, a wall of filing, meeting rooms pushed into the corners where two views meet.

It is worth saying plainly that most of the interior of the World Trade Center was ordinary. That is not a complaint, it is the fact that has been hardest to hold on to. A building remembered only through catastrophe loses its Tuesdays.
05The room at the top

One interior was not ordinary at all. Windows on the World opened on the hundred and sixth and hundred and seventh floors of the North Tower on 19 April 1976, across fifty thousand square feet designed by Warren Platner. Platner worked in brass, mirror and fabric covered walls, with tufted banquettes, discs set into the columns and dish shaped brass lights above them. Milton Glaser designed everything a guest touched or read: the dinnerware, the rugs, the light fittings, the menus. Paul Goldberger called the result sensuous modernism, which was accurate and, at the time, faintly disapproving.

The clever move was structural rather than decorative. Platner stepped the dining room in tiers, so that the view through that eighteen inch glass belonged to every table instead of to the row beside the window. A jacket was required and the restaurant kept a rack of them for men who arrived without one. On the south side sat the Cellar in the Sky, a small room with a fixed menu and its own wine list. After the 1993 bombing the space was rebuilt for twelve and a half million dollars and reopened on 26 June 1996. In its last full year it took thirty seven million dollars and was the highest grossing restaurant in the United States.

Around the dining room sat the rest of it: a wine school that ran for decades under Kevin Zraly, and on the hundred and seventh floor the Hors d'Oeuvrerie, which in the nineties became the Greatest Bar on Earth, full length windows and a dance floor. The bomb of February 1993 went off in the garage six levels down, and it was the underground that took it, the concourse and the station and the plant. The towers stood, but the restaurant at the top stayed shut for three years.
The tiers were the design. A window that narrow gives the view to whoever sits closest, unless the floor itself is arranged to hand it back.
06What hung in the lobbies

Art was distributed through the interiors as deliberately as the elevators. In the lobby of the South Tower hung a tapestry made by Joan Miro with Josep Royo, wool and hemp, twenty feet by thirty five and four tons of it, in place from 1974. On the mezzanine of the North Tower stood Louise Nevelson's Sky Gate, New York, black painted wood, finished in 1978. Alexander Calder's red stabile stood outside on the north side of the site, and Masayuki Nagare's Cloud Fortress sat on the plaza itself, a low black granite mass that people used as a wall to sit against. At the centre of the plaza fountain, Fritz Koenig's bronze Sphere turned once every twenty four hours, slowly enough that you could not watch it move and surely enough that it was never quite where you had left it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvi6zcaxgbauu.jpg
content.caption: Austin J. Tobin Plaza from above, with Fritz Koenig’s Sphere at the centre of the fountain. The bronze turned a full circle every twenty four hours.
content.credit: Photo: Balthazar Korab, public domain, via the Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvi70bwhbgbsp.jpg
content.caption: Masayuki Nagare’s Cloud Fortress on the plaza, with the perimeter columns rising behind it.
content.credit: Photo: Balthazar Korab, public domain, via the Library of Congress and Wikimedia Commons

content.content: 07The street underneath

Below all of this lay the part of the complex most people actually used. Six levels of substructure held a shopping concourse, the PATH station, parking and the plant that ran the towers. The plaza above was exposed and frequently unkind in wind, so the mall became the real street of the World Trade Center. For a great many people the building was entered from underneath, without ever crossing the open ground it was famous for.
08What is left

Tomorrow is the twenty fifth anniversary. Everything described here, with one exception, now exists only as description: the seventy four foot lobbies, the two sky lobbies, the acre floors, the brass and the tiers of Windows on the World, the tapestry, the Nevelson. Koenig's Sphere came through, dented and torn open, and stands today in Liberty Park a short walk from where it used to turn.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtvhpvfnn9mjj4.jpg
content.caption: The Sphere stood at the centre of the plaza fountain and turned once a day. Damaged and deliberately never repaired, it stands now in Liberty Park.
content.credit: Photo: Bernt Rostad, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

content.content: There is a habit of remembering buildings by their outlines, and it is convenient, because an outline has no rooms in it and therefore nobody inside. The World Trade Center was a place people went to work in the morning: through the concourse, up in an express car, out at a sky lobby, into a floor with a window eighteen inches wide. Keeping hold of that is not nostalgia about architecture. It is the only way the description stays about people.

Photographs, in order: the 107th floor of the North Tower in 1979 (Guerinf, CC BY-SA 3.0); the roof deck of the South Tower in 1984 (Lars Plougmann, CC BY-SA 2.0); the deck telescopes (Tequask, CC BY-SA 4.0); the entrance arches, the lobby under construction in 1971, the plaza from above and Cloud Fortress (Balthazar Korab and Warren K. Leffler, public domain, Library of Congress); the Sphere in Liberty Park (Bernt Rostad, CC BY 2.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: Where the Souls Become Cranes
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Nataliia Maloh
articles.excerpt: Nataliia Maloh, painter and curator, on her anniversary exhibition at ArtLab, the space she built from nothing on the shore of Lake Maggiore, and why she believes the deepest bridges between cultures come from the fact that none of them has ever been one thing.

content.content: Verbania sits on the shore of Lake Maggiore, in Piedmont, in the shadow of the Alps. At Via Baiettini 53, in a space that did not exist eighteen months ago, thirty five paintings by thirty five Ukrainian artists now hang under the title Ukraine. A Memory That Continues, one work for every year of Ukraine's independence, on view from 24 August through 30 September 2026.
