The space is called ArtLab, and it belongs to Nataliia Maloh, a Ukrainian painter and curator who arrived in Italy as an emigrant, found seasonal work, lost a winter to unemployment, and used the four idle months that followed to finally do what she had spent years postponing in a Kyiv office during her lunch breaks: paint.

The exhibition did not begin with the paintings. It began with a story Maloh wanted to tell, of land, of mothers, of cranes rising over cities left behind, and only afterward did she go looking for the works that could carry each part of it. The result reads less like a survey than a book, one canvas per page: a section called Madre Terra, Mother Earth, on the fields that fed generations and are now mined or occupied; a mother giving her sons a last kiss before their souls lift away as cranes; Italian landscapes that stand, in the show, as a quiet thank you to the country that took Ukrainians in.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/souls-cranes-hero-35.jpg
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8tobl2jmtnrl.jpg
content.caption: Da sinistra a destra: Luciano Paretti – Assessore alla Cultura della Città di Verbania. Olena Gryshchenko – Console d’Ucraina presso il Consolato Generale d’Ucraina a Milano. Giovanni Rodari – Consigliere comunale della Città di Verbania. Marisa Cortese – Curatrice e critica d’arte. Nataliia Maloholovko – Fondatrice del progetto “ArtLab by Nataliia Maloh” e organizzatrice della mostra “35. Ucraina. Una memoria che continua”. Olha Pylypenko – Vice Console presso il Consolato Generale d’Ucraina a Milano.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mty3k2t4x7a0qk.jpg
content.caption: "Madre Ucraina," the work that gives its name to the exhibition’s central section. Courtesy ArtLab. Anastasiia Hrudka, "Teneri abbracci," 2024, acrilico su tela, 70×55 cm

content.content: We spoke with Maloh about the half basement room in Italy where she first picked up a brush again, the stranger at a Christmas market who pointed her toward the local art association, and why she believes the deepest cultural bridge between Ukraine and Italy has nothing to do with the two countries at all, and everything to do with the fact that neither of them has ever been culturally one thing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8todkxyrvj4a.jpg
content.caption: Intervento di Luciano Paretti, Assessore alla Cultura della Città di Verbania, durante l’inaugurazione della mostra. Alla sua sinistra: Olena Gryshchenko – Console d’Ucraina presso il Consolato Generale d’Ucraina a Milano; Nataliia Maloholovko – Fondatrice del progetto “ArtLab by Nataliia Maloh” e organizzatrice della mostra “35. Ucraina. Una memoria che continua”. Opera sullo sfondo: Anzhelika Volkanova, “Volo verso sé stessi,” 2025, olio su tela, 90×120 cm.

content.content: Let's start with your own story. How did your path in art take shape, from your first creative instincts to your practice, your curatorial work, and your life in Italy? Was there a moment after which you stopped seeing yourself only as a painter, and began seeing yourself as someone who could build a space for other artists?
I can point to three moments that probably describe my path best.

The first is still in Ukraine. I had a normal office job in the city centre, nine to six, and during lunch breaks I kept finding myself in an art supply shop, buying paints and brushes and sketchbooks I would carry home and put in a cupboard, telling myself I would get to them eventually. Spoiler: in Ukraine, I never did.

The second is already in Italy. I worked through the summer season, and when it ended I registered for unemployment benefits. At some point it struck me, quite simply, that I was being paid and had four free months ahead of me, which meant I could finally do the thing I had wanted to do for years. I set up a small corner for myself in the half basement of the house we lived in. It was about thirteen degrees in there, so I worked in a coat, but after that there was no going back.

The third moment was my entry into the local Italian art scene, and it happened almost by accident. For a long time I thought nothing was happening in our city, no listings, no posters for anything interesting, apart from the Christmas markets. So I found out, stubbornly, who organised them, what paperwork I needed, even borrowed a proper market tent since they all had to match. I turned up at the 2024 Christmas market on the lakefront with a fifty by fifty sign, in Italian: “Looking for a place to exhibit my flower paintings.” At some point the town eccentric walked up, gave me the name and address of an association, and told me to go there. That chance encounter is, in fact, how I entered the local art world.

The desire and the ability to build something for other artists, I think, comes largely from my earlier professional life. In Ukraine I organised events for international technical assistance projects, so running an event, connecting people, carrying an idea from concept to execution, was a craft I already knew well before I ever thought of art as a profession. At some point those two halves of my life simply met: the need to create, and the experience of organising and bringing people together. That is when I understood that I was interested not only in making my own work, but in making a space where other artists could be seen.

What place has Italy come to occupy in your story? What changed in your understanding of art once you encountered Italian culture: its relationship to history, beauty, urban space, local heritage and everyday life? And has that experience changed how you look at Ukraine?
Italy, quite literally, warmed me. That is probably the most accurate way I can put it.

The sun here is so warm and there is so much light that at some point it became impossible to keep living and working the way I had before. When I first arrived I carried on, for a while, with the kind of work I had brought with me from Ukraine. But I started to feel a real dissonance: sun, a lake, mountains, extraordinary beauty, a completely different pace of life all around me, and I was still sitting in front of a computer, on the old script. At some point I simply asked myself: why keep doing something that no longer brings me joy, when life itself seems to be pushing me toward the thing I always wanted to do? So I consciously gave up my old work, and art arrived very naturally in its place, first the wish to paint, and later the wish to help other artists find their own way into the Italian art world.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8tohywr3lc1d.jpg
content.caption: Inaugurazione della mostra, 24 agosto 2026. ArtLab, Verbania, Italia.

content.content: Italy also changed how I see art itself. Here it does not exist apart from everyday life. It is in the architecture, on the streets, in small churches, old buildings, town squares. What struck me most, though, is how many ordinary people practise art in one form or another. A nurse, a doctor, a shop assistant can work all day at their profession and come home in the evening to paint, work in ceramics, take photographs, make music, make something with their hands, and nobody asks whether they are a real artist. Creativity is woven into life here in a very natural way. I think that gave me a kind of inner freedom: art does not have to start with permission, a diploma, or the day you decide to call yourself an artist. You can simply begin, because it is a need, and see where the path takes you.

I am also drawn to how carefully people here treat local history and heritage. Even a small town or a small association can have its own cultural tradition that people maintain and consider important. Which is probably why I started looking at Ukraine differently. When you live far from it, you begin to see, more sharply, the value of things that once seemed ordinary: our culture, our history, our local traditions. And you start wanting not just to talk about Ukraine, but to create opportunities for people to see it through art. What matters to me is that this should not run in one direction only, not just showing Ukrainian art inside my own space, but Ukrainian artists gradually entering the Italian cultural environment itself, meeting local artists, associations and curators, taking part in exhibitions beyond ArtLab. A simple example: today, 11 September, another exhibition opens featuring an artist whose work is currently showing at ArtLab as part of this show. That, to me, is one of the most important results of this work: when an acquaintance that began in my space goes on to have a life of its own in the wider Italian art scene.

So when I say Italy warmed me, it is not just a metaphor. I sometimes think it was literally the sun and the light here that pulled me out of my old life and made me ask myself a very simple question: if you have finally ended up somewhere good, why not let yourself do what you actually love? For me, the answer was art.

ArtLab in Verbania joins your own initiative with curatorial and public work. What cultural need was missing when the idea for ArtLab came to you? And what do you want the project to become in the long run: an exhibition space, a laboratory of exchange, a meeting point between cultures, or a mediator between artist, city and community?

It is simple and complicated at once. When I arrived in Verbania, one of my first impulses was to find a gallery and see contemporary Italian art. To my surprise, a Google Maps search for the whole city turned up almost nothing. Later, once I got to know the local scene better, I found the annual shows, the announcements for collective projects, the artists and associations. The art life here does exist, it is just somewhat fragmented. What was genuinely missing was a permanent, open space where contemporary art and the public could meet regularly. And it turned out I was not the only one who felt that. After ArtLab's first exhibition opened this July, many visitors told me almost the same thing: the town had been missing exactly this kind of place.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mty3k0aq6lriz2.jpg
content.caption: Inside ArtLab, Via Baiettini 53, Verbania. Courtesy of ArtLab. Olha Kovalyk, “Sera” – l’eco delle case lasciate in Ucraina rimane per sempre nella nostra memoria. 2025, olio su tela, 80×50 cm.

content.content: So I would not want to limit ArtLab to the word “gallery.” For me it is first of all a living space, one where art can be shown, but where it is just as important to introduce people to each other, to build new connections, to give artists the chance to be seen and heard. In the long run, I would like ArtLab to become a genuine meeting point: between artist and viewer, between the city and contemporary art, between different cultural environments, and, for me personally, above all between Ukraine and Italy. I like the idea that ArtLab does not have to be an endpoint for an artist, but rather a place where something begins for them: a new acquaintance, participation in another show, a collaboration with a local association or curator, a new project. When that happens, ArtLab is doing exactly what I built it to do: not just hanging art on a wall, but building an environment around it.

Italy is hard to understand through the idea of a single national culture. Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, Tuscany, Sardinia and Sicily each carry their own historical memory and visual language. Ukraine, too, is made up of many local cultural experiences. Do you see a shared model between the two countries, in which national identity is born not from flattening regional difference, but from preserving it?

Oh, absolutely, and it is one of the things about Italy that fascinates me most. Local identity here is extraordinarily strong. Dialects differ from region to region, sometimes entire regional languages differ, along with tradition, cuisine and architecture. A person can feel deeply Piedmontese, Sicilian, Venetian or Sardinian, and still be entirely Italian. There are other interesting parallels too. Many southern Italians have long moved north for work and better economic prospects, so within one country there are very different historical, social and economic experiences.

And yet, alongside all of that, “Italian-ness” is everywhere. Made in Italy, the tricolour, you see them on clothes, products, packaging, signage, even, absurdly, on a box of eggs. Behind it is a very clear message: this is ours, made here, and we are proud of it. Regional difference does not undermine national identity here. If anything, it seems to fill it. Italians are keenly aware of the enormous historical inheritance of their land, from antiquity and Rome to each region's own traditions, and they treat all of it as shared cultural capital.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/souls-cranes-girl-bird.jpg
content.caption: Parte dell’esposizione dedicata al commovente addio delle madri ai propri figli. Courtesy of ArtLab.

content.content: That is where I really see a parallel with Ukraine. We too have never been culturally uniform, and I do not think we need to become so. Hutsulshchyna does not have to resemble Slobozhanshchyna, Odesa does not have to resemble Poltava, Zakarpattia does not have to resemble Donetsk. Every region has its own history, intonation, architecture, cuisine, music, tradition, even its own sense of space. I think the strength of a national culture lies not in making everyone the same, but in learning to see that difference as shared wealth. Perhaps that is what Italy has additionally taught me: you can love your small corner of a country deeply, protect its dialect, its traditions, its history, and it does not contradict a strong national identity at all. On the contrary, when a person knows exactly what they bring to the shared culture, that shared culture becomes stronger. I would like us to look at Ukraine the same way: not trying to erase our differences for the sake of unity, but understanding that Ukraine is precisely made of them.

The Italian idea of territorio joins geography, architecture, craft, landscape, family memory and a way of life. For Ukraine, after occupation, displacement and the destruction of cities, the bond between a person and a specific place has taken on particular weight. Could this category become one of the languages through which an Italian viewer comes to understand contemporary Ukrainian art more deeply?

Yes, absolutely. The exhibition has a section called Madre Terra, Mother Earth, and through it I try to explain to Italian visitors that for a Ukrainian, land is far more than territory in the geographic sense. I talk about our fields, the fertility of Ukrainian soil, the symbolism of our flag's colours, blue sky over golden wheat fields, and then explain that today part of those fields is occupied, part is mined, part is contaminated by the war. Land that fed generations becomes, literally, dangerous to human life. I think Italians understand this through territorio particularly well, because there is also a very strong emotional bond here between a person and their land, their city, their house, their local landscape.

But in this exhibition I try to speak less in the language of facts than in the language of symbols and universal human emotion. I talk about the war through the image of a mother giving her sons a last kiss, their souls lifting away as cranes into eternity. You do not need to be Ukrainian to understand that image, or even to know the history of this war in detail. Almost everyone, in their own life, has lost someone, and knows what the pain of loss feels like, and so can come close, at least emotionally, to what Ukrainian mothers losing their children are living through today.

One moment at the exhibition stayed with me. An Italian woman came in with her three children, and as I told her about this work, the cranes, the mother, the last kiss, I watched her eyes fill with tears. In that moment I understood I had given her something far larger than information about the war in Ukraine.

That is why I believe so strongly in symbolism. Symbols do not need translating the way words do. Land, home, mother, child, road, water, bird, parting, return: these are images that exist in almost every culture. I do not think I could convey the Ukrainian experience to an Italian viewer as well through dates and figures and chronology as I can through the image of land you love and might lose, a home you cannot return to, a mother saying goodbye to her child. Through these, the distance between the Ukrainian and the Italian experience suddenly becomes much smaller. So yes, territorio can be one such language. But more broadly, I would say art lets you speak about a very specific Ukrainian experience through universal human feeling. And that is the moment a viewer stops treating Ukraine as something distant they hear about in the news, and starts to feel it through their own life.

The exhibition's title itself treats memory not as a finished past but as a process. When you present Ukrainian artists to an Italian audience, how do you handle the difficult curatorial problem of speaking about the war and the contemporary Ukrainian experience, without letting the war become the only lens through which Europe reads Ukrainian culture?

I try to speak through symbols and emotions available to anyone, regardless of nationality. Everyone has lost someone, so everyone can understand the pain of the thousands of Ukrainian mothers saying goodbye to their sons today. I speak about Ukrainian land through the image of a woman in a field, the earth as mother, as the source of life, as part of our identity. I speak about forced emigration through cranes rising over cities and fields, leaving familiar places behind and setting out in search of a new home. Through Italian landscapes I thank Italy and Italians for the shelter they gave us, and tell the story of how many of us found a second home here. But alongside that there remains a memory of the first one. In our memory the echo of our apartment blocks lives on, our familiar streets, the lights of our cities, all the everyday life we left behind one day.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8tof78k0nxlt.jpg
content.caption: Angolo dedicato al sottotema “Madre Terra” – la terra madre che nutre, protegge e offre rifugio.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8tog7v50ojdm.jpg
content.caption: La sofferenza delle donne che danno l’ultimo bacio ai propri figli, le cui anime volano verso l’eternità trasformandosi in gru. Khrystyna Pasichna, “Le donne mirofore,” 2025, tempera, gesso, tavola, 47×60 cm.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8toh491py7hb.jpg
content.caption: Le cicogne simboleggiano il processo dell’emigrazione: si sono alzate in volo, lasciandosi alle spalle le proprie case. Nataliia Berezniak, “La cicogna sopra l’Ucraina,” 2026, acrilico e foglia d’oro su tela, 80×60 cm. Iryna Winnik, “L’inizio di marzo. Ucraina,” 2026, acrilico su tela, 60×60 cm.

content.content: So the war is present in this exhibition, and it would be dishonest to try to avoid it. It is today part of the Ukrainian experience. But for me it is essential that Ukraine is not represented only through war, destruction and death. Ukraine in this show is also land, home, motherhood, love, memory, the road, the search for a new home, the ability to begin life again. It is longing for what was left behind, and gratitude toward those who took us in. It is a country living through war, whose culture did not begin with that war and will not end with it.

The exhibition itself was built in a somewhat unusual way. First I had the story I wanted to tell, and only afterward did I start choosing the works to fit under it, moving from concept to painting rather than the other way round. Each work became something like an illustration of one part of that story, almost like an image in a book: one speaks of land, another of loss, the next of emigration, of the search for home, of memory, of hope. Together they form one continuous narrative. That is probably why the title carries the words “a memory that continues.” Memory, for me, is not only what stayed in the past. It keeps shaping our present: how we see new places, how we build a new home, how we perceive the people around us, and how we tell our own story to others. I would like an Italian visitor to leave not simply thinking, “I saw an exhibition about the war in Ukraine,” but feeling: “I understand a little better the people living through this, and the country they carry with them.”

Ukraine and Italy share unexpectedly many structural parallels: strong craft traditions, a cult of material, local schools, sacred art, knowledge passed down through families, a particular weight given to home and land. At the same time, twentieth century Italian art, Arte Povera in particular, taught artists to treat simple materials as carriers of memory and meaning. Where do you personally see the most interesting ground for a genuine Ukrainian Italian artistic dialogue, one that goes beyond formal cultural diplomacy and surface resemblance?

I think the most interesting dialogue begins exactly where we stop deliberately looking for similarities between Ukraine and Italy. Cultural diplomacy often works to a familiar formula: bring Ukrainian art, show it to an Italian audience, talk about Ukraine, and the meeting of the two cultures more or less ends there. That is not enough for me. I am far more interested in creating a situation where a Ukrainian and an Italian artist end up in the same space and start talking about things that matter to both, but each from their own cultural experience. It could be the theme of home, land, memory, family, migration, loss, water, landscape. Even the same material can carry an entirely different memory in two cultures. Earth means something different to a Piedmontese artist and to a Ukrainian one, and it is precisely that difference that creates a real dialogue.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8tojydof5t65.jpg
content.caption: Inaugurazione della mostra, 24 agosto 2026. ArtLab, Verbania, Italia.

content.content: I find it especially interesting to work not only with the big national categories of “Ukraine” and “Italy,” but to move down to a local level. For example, placing side by side the experience of a Ukrainian artist for whom the steppe, the field or an industrial city matters, and an artist from the shores of Lake Maggiore, for whom the formative childhood images are mountains, water, stone, small old towns, and seeing what emerges between those two experiences. The same applies to craft and material. I am deeply drawn to the idea that an ordinary thing, wood, cloth, metal, stone, earth, an old object, can be not just material to work with, but a carrier of memory. There is a great deal of common ground between Ukrainian and Italian traditions here, without needing to force the resemblance. That is why it matters to me that ArtLab gradually becomes more than a place where Italians are shown Ukrainian artists. I would like to build genuine Ukrainian Italian projects, where artists work around a single theme but speak about it each in their own language. Real cultural dialogue, for me, is not when we say “look how alike we are,” and it is not one culture explaining itself to another. It begins when two different cultures ask each other questions, and each ends up seeing itself a little differently as a result.

Much of today's Ukrainian European cultural connection is, understandably, built around support and solidarity. But what should come next? If you imagined a permanent cultural route between Ukraine and Italy, between artists, small towns, workshops, independent spaces and local communities, what shared questions would you build it around? And what role could ArtLab play in that longer term dialogue?

I think the next important step is the move from support and solidarity toward a full professional exchange. Today, quite understandably, many Ukrainian cultural projects in Europe arise in the context of war and the wish to support Ukraine, and we are endlessly grateful for that support. But in the long run, I would like a Ukrainian artist to be invited not because they represent a country at war, but because they are interesting as an artist: for their language, their ideas, their technique, their way of seeing the world.

That is why I see real potential in ongoing exchange: residencies, joint exhibitions, exchanges between artists, workshops, independent spaces and local communities. I am particularly interested in the level of small towns. Cultural exchange does not have to happen only between Kyiv, Milan or Rome. Small towns have their own memory, cultural energy, their own artists and their own audience. I would build such a route around very simple and universal questions: what does home mean to us? How does the place where we were born or live shape who we are? How do we hold on to memory? What happens to a person when they change countries? How can tradition live inside contemporary art? How does a local culture become part of a global one without losing its own voice?

In that system, I see ArtLab as one small point on a much larger cultural route. In the long term, I would like to expand ArtLab's format into an artist residency, so I could invite artists from around the world, and especially from Ukraine, to live and work here for a time, meet local artists and cultural institutions, exchange experience and create joint projects. And I have one further goal: for ArtLab to become a kind of springboard for Ukrainian artists into the international art world. Not a place where an artist shows one work once, but a place after which the next contact, the next exhibition, the next collaboration follows. That work, in fact, is already under way. Over time, I would like us to talk less about “supporting Ukrainian art” and more about its natural presence in the European cultural space. For me, that will be the real sign that we have moved from solidarity to a genuine, long term cultural dialogue.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mty3k15n2d6hdg.jpg
content.caption: Visitors during a guided tour of “Ukraine. A Memory That Continues.” Courtesy ArtLab

content.content: Ukraine. A Memory That Continues (35. Ucraina. Una memoria che continua) is on view at ArtLab, Via Baiettini 53, Verbania (VB), Italy, from 24 August to 30 September 2026. Guided visits are available by appointment.

articles.title: Architecture That Listens
articles.author: US Architecture Studio
articles.excerpt: How multi-layered context shapes identity across three projects by US Architecture Studio, from a steppe town, through rolling hills, to a small cafe.

content.content: Architecture is something considerably larger than physical walls. It is the ability to give material form to a place's memory, its climate, its habits, the routes people walk every day without thinking about them. A building that knows how to listen to its surroundings becomes a natural extension of the ground it stands on. From the open steppe of the east, through the textured hills of Galicia, to the restless center of the capital, the Ukrainian practice US Architecture Studio works from layered context rather than applied style, arriving at three different answers to the same underlying question. Three geographies, three projects.

A building's identity is not decoration added afterward. It is a precise spatial answer to the character of a place, one that gathers up meanings already latent in a site and makes them visible. Before drawing a single wall, the studio works through a set of deliberately basic questions: what is this plot? What does the street it sits on say? What is the town, the region, the culture around it? Does the result read as part of the country's own identity? The answers, an arid climate, a local domestic habit, the constant transit of a city block, end up shaping a building far more convincingly than any decoration laid on top of it afterward. What that method looks like in practice can be traced across three projects spanning very different parts of the country: the eastern steppe, the western landscape, and the pulsing center of the capital.
Svatove: the memory of a form

A private house on the outskirts of Svatove grew out of close study of the underlying logic, rather than the literal image, of traditional housing in the Luhansk region. The plot's narrow shape, together with local custom, climate and the historical proportions of the surrounding buildings, dictated a compact white volume set back from the road. To give the plan a livable, contemporary scale, the composition is completed by a contrasting dark block on the north side, its pitched roof kept visually unified by a single membrane covering. The overall form is further shaped by two carved out niches, one for a terrace, one for parking.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtyatjnabh3tw0.jpg
content.caption: The house's form, developed step by step from the proportions of local vernacular housing and a nearby historic settlement. Courtesy US Architecture Studio.

content.content: Tradition and continuity of form show up here in details easy to miss. The slender metal columns of the terrace and the parking canopy restate, in a new material, the idea of the old wooden porch post. Three differently sized windows on the white facade reinterpret a traditional local arrangement, and their placement sets up a wavelike rhythm that echoes the course of a nearby river. Inside, the plan avoids conventional corridors in favor of one continuous, flowing space: the kitchen and living room open upward into the second floor hall and its loggia. Working with the site's own slope, the house keeps its paved surface to a single driveway leading to the parking spot, leaving the rest of the plot free for a garden further up the hill.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtyatkdqe592c6.jpg
content.caption: Ground and second floor plans, Svatove. Courtesy US Architecture Studio.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu1iry08xjk5xr.jpg
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu1iryo9kiantx.jpg
Ternopil region: building from what was already there

Context is not only cultural or natural. On a plot in the Ternopil region, it was a literal constraint: an existing stone plinth and foundation left over from a generic house of the 2000s. That given became the starting point for a deliberately rational home, built for a family who chose to move out into the surrounding countryside. Every window and every square meter here answers directly to function. The restraint and the palette of the facades draw straight from vernacular building tradition, and the roof, a half hip form with a series of breaks in its slope, does most of the formal work.

That silhouette runs deep in the visual culture of Galicia and reads as instinctively familiar to anyone from the region. It also produces a far more articulated volume than a plain gable or hip roof would allow, while solving a purely practical problem: it keeps the attic usable at full height without resorting to dormer windows. Working with the site's pronounced slope, the house's strict practicality settles into something closer to comfort, and its local character grows directly out of function rather than being applied over it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtyatj6xyl1ris.jpg
content.caption: Ground and attic floor plans, a house in the Ternopil region built on an existing foundation. Courtesy US Architecture Studio.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu1irz9egabeg1.jpg
Kyiv: designing for a city in motion

In a large city, natural terrain and history are joined by something else: constant movement. A cafe project in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district sits inside a green strip along Povitrianykh Syl Avenue, wedged between student dormitories and university buildings that see a steady flow of foot traffic between them. The building answers that transit with a wavelike, insulating wall that shields the interior from the street, breaking its surface only once, for a single round window. The cafe's main visual draw is a heavy cantilevered roof whose wave motif carries inward, turning into a series of convex vaults overhead. The ceiling's dynamic vertical lines tie the terrace to the interior, running the length of the room and cutting into the wall behind the bar. That same shape structures the space outside too, setting a rhythm of three arches across the facade's glazing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtyathy1w4we2s.jpg
content.caption: Soloma, a cafe for Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, set inside a green strip along Povitrianykh Syl Avenue. Courtesy US Architecture Studio.

content.content: Inside, the column free volume splits visually into an intimate zone and a main hall offering five distinct ways to sit: half private nooks, a long communal table, a run of seats along the panoramic windows, and a central island of smaller tables. From outside, the building's overall geometry answers to the rhythm of traffic and pedestrians passing by, while a screen of existing trees gently separates it from the avenue. Inside, the main hall faces the opposite corner of the plot, keeping its calm and its open, panoramic view of the square across the street.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtyatihdm4zjzr.jpg
content.caption: Isolating the plot from the university grounds, then opening a visual line toward the square and the green beyond, before the cantilevered roof settles into its final form. Courtesy US Architecture Studio.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtyatirfl7dv8y.jpg
content.caption: Ground floor plan, Soloma. Courtesy US Architecture Studio.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu1irzvfo8mttc.jpg

A building that is genuinely alive always grows out of a deep reading of its place, its culture, its spatial surroundings, becoming a natural extension of the ground beneath it. It is exactly that connection that gives architecture real content, gives it a value that does not date, and makes the space around it easier to notice and understand.
US Architecture Studio is a Ukrainian practice working across architecture and identity consulting, and also runs the media project UkrArchStyle. More of their work: us-arch-studio.framer.website.

articles.title: Nothing Fallow About It: The Harvest Behind France's Novels and Italy's Golden Lion
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister
articles.excerpt: A Roman mosaic already knew what September was for. Two thousand years later France still times its book industry to it, and Italy still times its cinema to it. Nobody involved would call that a coincidence.

content.content: There is a month European culture never lets lie fallow. Long before anyone published a novel or projected a film, September was already booked: it is when southern Italy's vineyards come down off the vines, when the Roman calendar's own month-mosaics show two men treading grapes rather than resting, when an entire hemisphere's worth of agricultural labor gets crammed into six or seven weeks before the weather turns. Nothing about the modern versions of that instinct is new; only the crop has changed. France now harvests novels in September. Italy harvests films. Both still call the result a season.

• 461novels in the 2026 rentrée littéraire
  • 83rdedition of the Venice Film Festival
  • 1,800years since Rome carved the harvest into stone
A month that was never really free

The habit is older than either country's publishing house or festival jury. A third-century Roman mosaic from El Djem, in what is now Tunisia, gives September its own panel in a calendar of the months, and the panel shows two men treading grapes, not resting after summer. The tribute was to Bacchus, god of wine and, not incidentally, of the theater: the same god the Romans credited with both the vintage and the performance that celebrated it. In the south of Italy, where the heat breaks earlier, the vendemmia still runs through September; in the north, growers wait until November. The harvest and the calendar have simply never agreed to separate.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/92/Grape_harvesting_time_%281887%29%2C_by_Francesco_Gioli.jpg
content.caption: Grape Harvesting Time, Francesco Gioli, 1887 — Tuscan peasants at the vendemmia, painted a decade before cinema existed to compete with it.
content.credit: Francesco Gioli (1846–1922), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
content.alt: Painting of Tuscan peasants harvesting grapes, 1887

content.content: Caravaggio painted the same debt more directly, a decade before 1600: his Bacchus, now in the Uffizi, reclines with a wine glass in one hand and a wreath of vine leaves already loosening in his hair, unhurried in exactly the way the actual harvest never is. The painting has outlasted the empire that worshipped its subject by well over a thousand years. The vendemmia is older than both the empire and the painting, and has never needed either one's permission to keep arriving every September.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4f/Bacchus-Caravaggio_%281598%29.jpg
content.caption: Bacchus, Caravaggio, c. 1598, Uffizi Gallery, Florence.
content.credit: Michelangelo Merisi da Caravaggio, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
content.alt: Caravaggio's painting of Bacchus reclining with wine and grape leaves

content.content: France: the harvest moved from the vine to the shelf

France runs its own September harvest twice over, and rarely notices the overlap. Champagne's growers still call theirs the vendange; in 2026 an unusually mild winter and three summer heat waves pushed it earlier than anyone alive could remember, finishing by September 4 instead of dragging into the month as usual. The other harvest, the rentrée littéraire, keeps its own, stubborn calendar. The idea was already in the air by the 1880s, when the philosopher Ernest Renan first named the pattern, and the creation of the Prix Goncourt in 1903 gave publishers their first real reason to time a book's release around it. But the rentrée as anyone would recognize it today is a postwar invention: publishers only started clustering releases into a single autumn window in the late 1950s, once enough literary prizes were competing for the same November announcements to make August a wasted month. The 2026 rentrée counts 461 novels, 344 of them written in French, 117 translated, and 68 first novels, five fewer than the year before. The volume has been shrinking for a decade, but the deadline has not moved, because the deadline was never really about the books. It is about which of those 461 titles gets to stand in front of the Académie Goncourt's jury in November, and a book that arrives in October is already too late to be considered.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/cb/Librairie_La_Mouette_Rieuse_-_Paris_%2835176711825%29.jpg
content.caption: La Mouette Rieuse, a bookshop in Paris's Marais district, during a rentrée littéraire season.
content.credit: Photo: ActuaLitté, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
content.alt: Storefront of the Paris bookshop La Mouette Rieuse

content.content: Italy: the same instinct, dressed as a festival

Cinema's September ritual is younger than the vendemmia by about two thousand years and younger than the rentrée littéraire by roughly three decades, but it was built with the same appetite for spectacle Bacchus originally got the tribute for. The Venice International Film Festival opened in 1932 as an event within that year's Biennale, engineered by three men, Giuseppe Volpi, Luciano de Feo, and Antonio Maraini, who understood cinema's use as a projection of a modern, image-conscious Italy under Mussolini's government as clearly as they understood its box office. The first prize, introduced in 1934, was named the Coppa Mussolini; the festival went dark entirely from 1943 to 1945, then returned and, in 1949, replaced its old prize with the Golden Lion. The 83rd edition ran September 2 to 12, 2026, and gave that Lion to Woman Unknown, May el-Toukhy's Danish drama about a housemaid's wartime affair, under a jury led by Maggie Gyllenhaal. Ilya Khrzhanovsky took the Silver Lion for Best Director for DAU. George Clooney and Ellen Burstyn each received an honorary Golden Lion for lifetime achievement, the same honor the festival gave Werner Herzog the year before.
https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5f/Werner_Herzog_Venice_Film_Festival_2025.jpg
content.caption: Werner Herzog with his Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the 82nd Venice Film Festival, 2025.
content.credit: Photo: Colleen Sturtevant, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
content.alt: Werner Herzog holding his Golden Lion trophy

content.content: Paris will spend the next two months deciding which of four hundred and sixty-one novels get to matter. Venice has already spent its ten days deciding the same thing for a smaller, slower pool of films. Neither city would describe what it is doing as a harvest, and neither needs to: the metaphor was already carved into a mosaic in Roman Africa some seventeen centuries before either institution existed, and none of the three, the grape, the novel, or the film, has ever managed to make September optional.

articles.title: Diana Aleshchenko: Safety Comes From Openness
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Diana Aleshchenko
articles.excerpt: A new architecture graduate on a rehabilitation centre without right angles, a student campus built for wartime, and a courtyard that keeps the memory of July 1917 inside a railway hub.

content.content: Diana Aleshchenko is from Kyiv. This year she completed her master's degree in architecture and urban planning at the Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture (KNUBA), and her student portfolio already spans three very different briefs: a rehabilitation centre in Zhytomyr for people recovering from severe injury and trauma, a campus with student housing in Kharkiv, and a greenhouse complex at the Kyiv-Volynskyi railway hub.

What connects them is an insistence that every formal decision has to earn its place. The rounded walls in her rehabilitation centre are about wheelchairs and anxiety before they are about softness; the louvres on its façade are about who can see whom. EPRIS Journal asked her about the reasoning behind these projects, and about what it means to design for Ukrainian cities now.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eq1ka8wjapn.jpg
content.caption: Diana Aleshchenko with her project boards.

content.content: Tell us a little about yourself: where are you from, where did you study, and how did you come to architecture?

I'm from Kyiv, and this year I received my master's degree in architecture and urban planning at KNUBA in Kyiv. I don't have a unique story about a sudden childhood revelation after which I decided to tie my life to architecture. As I see it, the path took shape quite naturally and consistently: through a chain of my own decisions, a gradually growing interest in space, and specific life events that step by step brought me to where I am now.
What in your childhood or youth pushed you towards architecture in particular?

There wasn't a single childhood trigger that decided everything. It was more a gradual combination of interests in drawing, geometry and creative work, which with age simply turned into a conscious choice of profession.
How much did your studies at KNUBA shape your approach to design?

My studies gave me a clear understanding that learning never actually ends. From project to project you keep coming back to the point where you have to look for information again, research, find inspiration and endlessly rework decisions in search of form, all of it under tight deadlines. You start with one picture in your head and try to realise exactly that, but along the way everything transforms, and in the end something quite different is born, something much deeper. University taught me to keep up with that pace, to make decisions quickly and not to be afraid to let go of first ideas for the sake of a stronger final result.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eq40vwfi92h.jpg
content.caption: With a presentation model of one of her projects.

content.content: In your rehabilitation centre in Zhytomyr you chose bionic forms and rounded corners so that patients would feel safe. How did you decide which architectural devices genuinely create a sense of protection, rather than simply looking soft?

First of all, smooth, rounded, radial walls are far more comfortable to move along for a person in a wheelchair or with a prosthesis, where every corner is a potential obstacle. Given the specifics of the facility, and after analysing typical hospital plans with their 90-degree corners, we also took the psycho-emotional factor into account. For a person with acute stress disorder or PTSD, someone suddenly appearing from around a corner becomes an additional trigger for anxiety.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eq4e2kin3v3.jpg
content.caption: The rehabilitation centre in Zhytomyr. Angled metal louvres give patients privacy from the street while keeping the view open.

content.content: The metal louvres in the same project are angled so that patients can see the courtyard while passers-by on the street cannot see them. How did this solution come about, and were there options that didn't work?

From the very beginning we intended to make open balconies, so that a patient could get some fresh air without leaving their own room. But after consultations with specialists it became clear that for people with psychological trauma this is a dangerous solution. So the team held a brainstorm, looking for a way to keep the original idea, contact with the air and the forest, while making it completely safe. We tested full glazing and ordinary blinds, but they either created the feeling of a closed cell or blocked the view of nature entirely. Rotating louvres set at an angle turned out to be the best answer. They give the necessary privacy from the street, leave the patient a direct view of the courtyard and the pine forest, and at the same time allow the room to be aired comfortably without a sense of isolation. In the end this functional safety measure became the main visual feature of the whole façade.
The project was developed through consultations with medical staff at rehabilitation centres. Which of their advice changed the original concept the most?

Of course, the initial conceptual decisions were strongly influenced by the specifics of the building and research into its future users. We analysed different groups in detail, their particular needs and the real practice of how such facilities are arranged. During one of the consultations we were able to talk to a person who had created and improved rehabilitation centres in practice. The main insight of that conversation was an understanding of patients' psychological state and the specifics of their safety, and as a result we abandoned open balconies entirely. For ordinary housing or a hotel a balcony seems a natural choice, but for people undergoing rehabilitation after severe injuries, open cantilevered spaces create unnecessary anxiety and risk.

Your diploma project, a campus and student housing in Kharkiv, is built on a hybrid model: the ground floor becomes open public space, and the housing above is modular. Why this typology rather than the familiar corridor dormitory?

The ordinary corridor dormitory is long outdated and offers today's young people no new spatial experience. It shuts people away in narrow dark corridors, takes away the balance between socialising and privacy, and feels cut off from life. Active ground floors have long been an absolute must in good housing, and on a student campus they are even more critical. This is where an open public environment forms, with coworking spaces, shared areas and services, where students can easily make new contacts, meet classmates, exchange ideas and find like-minded people. The upper residential floors, meanwhile, are modular, so that every student has a proper personal place for focused study and rest. This hybrid typology works as a living student co-living: active socialising and integration into city life below, and a protected, ergonomic private space above.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eq4v6xtka94.jpg
content.caption: Campus and student housing in Kharkiv, master's project: an open, active ground floor with modular housing above.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eq5dldnfdbz.jpg
content.caption: Concept diagram: the shared public core of the campus among the surrounding blocks.

content.content: In one unit you place a sleeping loft to free up space for study; in another, a double, you create “vertical privacy” with a raised bed. How do you look for the balance between personal space and shared life in a student environment?

The balance between shared life and privacy starts with understanding that a person needs their own psychological territory, where their gaze and personal space do not constantly cross with others'. In a typical dormitory the beds stand on one horizontal plane, so a person is always in their neighbour's field of view, and that quickly wears you out. Vertical zoning and the sleeping mezzanine, which is the signature of the dormitory's layout, solve this problem. Raising the bed to a second level creates an individual capsule of quiet where you can completely switch off from what is happening in the room. In a single room this frees the lower level for a full workplace and for living without clutter, and in a double it gives the same vertical privacy, so that roommates don't disturb each other even within one space.

content.caption: Single and double units with a raised sleeping level.

content.content: This is a diploma project about Kharkiv, a city that now lives under constant wartime pressure. How much did that reality shape decisions in the project, directly or indirectly?

Without question, the reality of war significantly shaped the work, both in meaning and in planning. Despite constant shelling and danger, Kharkiv confidently remains among the top three cities in Ukraine by number of university applicants, which only confirms how relevant the choice of site is. The city lives, and young people want to study here. But designing for such a context using the old approaches is no longer possible. Safety became the defining factor for the whole structure of the complex, so a mandatory and fundamental part of the master's project was designing and calculating a spacious shelter. Not just a technical basement to tick a box, but a full underground space integrated into the functions of the campus.

content.caption: Illustration and axonometric detail from the Kharkiv campus project.

content.content: In your greenhouse project at the Kyiv-Volynskyi hub, you write about a transition from fast, noisy transit to calm and focus. How did you achieve that transition architecturally, rather than just marking it on a plan?

The transition from transit to calm is achieved above all through a clear sequence of physical barriers. Between the noisy railway and the calm that the greenhouse stands for there is not just distance. First comes a separate block of the building and an open space in front of it, which take the first wave and physically damp the main sound from the trains. Only after passing this buffer does a person come under the rhythm of pergolas and covered galleries, where the form of the complex itself begins to work as a protective contour. Low horizontal volumes and dense planting fully screen the central zone from city noise and visual chaos. The change of scale, the shade of the pergola and the green mass shift attention from the bustle of transit to quiet, creating a natural insulation around the greenhouse before a person even crosses its threshold.

content.caption: The complex at the Kyiv-Volynskyi hub: functional zoning and master plan.

content.content: The inner courtyard of the same project is dedicated to the memory of the events of 1917. Where did this idea come from, and how did you work with such a sensitive subject in a space that remains a transport hub?

Any design for me begins with thorough pre-design analysis. Not only of the terrain or the surroundings, but also of the historical heritage of the site. Once I received the brief, I began my research with exactly this part of the urban analysis, looking for an initial hook from which the concept and idea of the project could develop. Few passengers realise it, but it was here, at Post-Volynskyi station, that on 26 July 1917 Russian military units opened machine-gun fire on the train of the Bohdan Khmelnytsky Regiment as it was leaving for the front. It was a tragic and symbolic starting point of the Ukrainian struggle for liberation, and it happened on these very tracks.

Working with such a subject inside a transport hub is an extremely complex and responsible task. A station lives by transit, bustle and speed. So the memory of these events and the idea of resilience are built into the heart of the complex: the inner courtyard with the greenhouse and the rhythmic structure of pergolas. This green core is the main spatial and acoustic buffer. Coming here from dynamic transit, a person finds themselves in a protected space of calm where the rumble of the railway is cut off. The greenhouse and living nature under the pergola speak of memory in the language of life, light and renewal, giving passengers the choice to rest from the noise of the city, to slow down, or to reflect on the historical weight of the place beneath their feet.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eq97rneasea.jpg
content.caption: Axonometry of the complex beside the railway, with the inner courtyard at its centre.

content.content: Most of your projects have very expressive graphics and atmospheric renders. Where, for you, is the line between showing architecture convincingly and letting the image become a work in its own right?

For me architectural visualisation is first of all photographic art. I don't look at it as computer graphics for the sake of special effects, but the way a photographer does who arrives at a building and looks for the right angle, feels the light, the air, the tactility of materials and the mood.

The line between being convincing and a picture that exists for its own sake runs where honesty towards the project begins. A photograph can be deep, atmospheric and artistic, but its task is to capture and reveal the real character of the environment. When a render works as an honest frame from the life of a future building, it helps a person feel the space before it is even built.

content.caption: Visualisations from Diana Aleshchenko's portfolio.

content.content: If you had to defend one of these projects before a jury asking uncomfortable questions, which decision would you defend most fiercely, and which would you admit is weak?

If I had to defend the Kharkiv campus again before a critical jury, I would most fiercely defend the decision to make the ground floor a fully active, open, multifunctional space for all residents of the city. So that a building with a sports complex or a swimming pool lives not only in the first half of the day during classes, but also in the evenings and during the holidays. The jury would probably appeal to traditional ideas about safety: that a student environment should be isolated, behind a fence. But I am convinced that closedness does not make a place safe. Safety comes from openness, from living contact with the neighbourhood, from social control and the constant presence of people on the street.

The decision I am ready to see openly criticised is the spatial optimisation of the compact units with a raised sleeping place. Although it solves the problem of privacy on a limited floor area, it is always a compromise in terms of universal inclusivity: a sleeping mezzanine suits young, mobile people, but creates a barrier for students with limited mobility.
What, in your view, distinguishes Ukrainian architectural education and the young architectural community right now?

Above all, a striking cohesion and a readiness to keep generating ideas and creating something new, whatever the external circumstances. Watching today's students, graduates, my classmates and colleagues, I see enormous inner resilience and professional courage. Our generation is being formed in exceptionally difficult conditions, but this has not broken our interest in the profession; on the contrary, it has sharpened our sense of responsibility and the quality of the projects. Right now the Ukrainian architectural community is raising very strong, competitive and thoughtful specialists who are ready to work with the most complex spatial and social challenges.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eqbnzspfrsx.jpg
content.caption: Graduates with their project boards.

content.content: Tell us about something that has inspired you recently: a project, a place, a person.

For me music, film and photography are not just a source of emotion but a real foundation for architectural decisions. Any creative work around you can become an unexpected impulse for a space. One recent example was the concept of one of my master's projects, inspired by Ariana Grande's album and the film of the same name, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind. I really love that process, when a sincere personal passion turns into an unconventional architectural idea.
How do you see your architectural career from here?

I definitely see my future development within the Ukrainian architectural community. I want to create, to rebuild, and to do everything possible so that space in our home cities is inspiring, alive and safe for people. It matters to me to invest my experience and vision in an environment that truly matters and needs real change here and now.

content.caption: Diana Aleshchenko with her work.

content.content: What advice would you give yourself at the start of your studies?

Keep training your eye, don't stop at the first successful option and keep generating, because the best solutions often appear after you thought the search was over. And a purely practical piece of advice: move to digital tools and computer graphics as early as possible, and keep figuring out the new functions and tricks of the software. The more freely you handle the software, the more precisely and quickly you can realise any spatial idea.
Visualisations and drawings: Diana Aleshchenko. Interview conducted in writing for EPRIS Journal, September 2026.

articles.title: Oksana Dzhuman: A Self-Portrait in 5,500 Sticks
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & Oksana Dzhuman
articles.excerpt: The Valencia-based artist on turning used tobacco sticks into mosaic portraits, painting each one by hand, and showing the work to the public for the first time at Russafa Art.

content.content: Oksana Dzhuman trained as an interior designer, then studied graphic design, then spent several years as a tattoo artist. Today she lives in Valencia and works as an artist, repeatedly returning to an unusual material: used tobacco sticks, disinfected, painted individually by hand and assembled into large mosaic portraits.

The series began at the end of 2024 with a small box on her table. Her largest work so far, a self-portrait, is made from around 5,500 sticks. In 2026 the mosaics were shown publicly for the first time, at Russafa Art in Valencia. EPRIS Journal spoke with her about the long road to this material, the process behind a single portrait, and the painting she calls La Guerra.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8ssvil8j0lq5.jpg
content.caption: Oksana Dzhuman with one of her mosaics.

content.content: You trained as an interior designer, then studied graphic design, and today you work as an artist in Valencia. How did these different stages of study and experience shape the way you see composition, form and space in your work?

At university, I wasn't exactly the most serious student. I realised quite quickly that interior design itself didn't really interest me, and if an assignment didn't grab me, I did it simply because it had to be done.

But there was one exercise I really liked. We had to paint sheets of paper ourselves in different shades, cut them into small squares and rectangles, and assemble an image from them. I made two ravens sitting on a branch in purple tones. Only now do I realise how close it was to what I do today, just with a completely different material.

Later I went to study graphic design. That was already part of searching for what I wanted to do, but in the end that wasn't mine either. After that I came to tattooing and worked in that field for several years. I think that experience influenced me much more strongly. Tattooing definitely taught me patience, attention to detail and how to work with composition.
Looking back, your path in art reads like several different chapters: drawing, tattoo, and now portraits from recycled materials. How do you connect these chapters into one story for yourself?

For a long time I didn't see it as one story at all. I was constantly trying something new: I could get absorbed in one thing, then switch to something completely different, and after a while come back to something again.

Only when the mosaics appeared did I start looking back and noticing things that repeat. I have always loved details, long manual work, colour, and the process itself, when a whole gradually emerges from separate elements.

And that pull appeared even before university. At school, I remember spending a whole night covering my phone by hand with hundreds of tiny rhinestones, inventing the pattern as I went and not noticing the time at all. Later the phone was, fittingly, stolen. Perhaps all that sparkle did its job after all.
So now I see it all as a rather chaotic path, in which only after years did I begin to listen to myself more and understand what I actually love.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eqe6c7s109s.jpg
content.caption: The phone she covered in rhinestones over one night as a schoolgirl.

content.content: Do you remember the moment you first thought that an ordinary used stick could become something more than rubbish? What caught your attention then?

It all began at the end of 2024, unfortunately, with smoking. I kept a small box nearby and started collecting used sticks in it. That was when I first noticed how quickly they accumulated. When you stop seeing them as one or two sticks you simply throw away and instead see how many collect in just a few days, you become uncomfortably aware of the scale of your own habit.

That same evening I started looking at the sticks themselves, and at some point something just clicked: what if I tried to make something out of them? The idea came very suddenly, almost like a light bulb switching on. They were waste, there were a lot of them, and they were small, light and all the same shape. I immediately wanted to know whether they could become a material to work with.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eqeipslkuyn.jpg
content.caption: The first box of used sticks.

content.content: At first your works were made only from your own sticks, but over time other people began to join the project. How did that happen naturally, and what changed for you personally when the material stopped being only yours?

Until 2026 I used only my own sticks, so collecting material took a very long time. The first person to help me was a Spanish friend of mine, and I'm very grateful to her for the support. Then other people gradually joined in, and there was noticeably more material.

Later I posted on social media that I was collecting used sticks for my work, and unexpectedly quite a lot of people responded. People even gave me whole cartons of new sticks. It changed the pace of the work a great deal: before, I had to wait for months until enough material piled up for one piece, and now several thousand sticks can be collected much faster.

And I now see the works themselves a little differently. I look at them and understand that they are no longer made only from my own material. In a sense, many people take part in making each of them, and I'm very grateful to everyone who helps me collect it.

content.caption: Material arrives from friends and followers: packs, bags and whole collections.

content.content: If we take our time and describe the whole journey of one work, from the first stick to the finished portrait, which part of the process gives you the most pleasure, and which demands the most patience?
It all starts with collecting. Then comes a rather long preparation process: several stages of disinfection and treatment to remove the smell.
While the sticks are being treated, I prepare the canvas at the same time: I make the layout and a colour map, so I understand which shades I'll need and roughly how the work will look.

Then I paint the sticks in the shades I need. Many people are surprised that I paint every stick by hand, but for me this is the most meditative part of the process. After that, I begin assembling the image on the canvas.
The whole process requires patience, but preparing the material probably takes the most. It takes quite a lot of time.

content.caption: From sorted material to painted rows: stages of a work in progress.

content.content: You assembled your self-portrait from 5,500 painted sticks; it is the largest work in the series. If it isn't too personal a question: what did you feel as you gradually recognised your own face in this unusual technique?

While I work, I almost can't see the image. The canvases are large, and you work with them however you can: from the side, from above, sometimes almost lying down. Up close it all looks like a set of separate shades, and the image simply doesn't come together. You can only understand what's emerging by stepping back. With the self-portrait it was even harder, because it is practically black and white.

And when the work was finished, the emotions were very mixed. I was glad I'd finished it, I was proud of myself, and at the same time I wanted to cry and not show it to anyone at all. I think the realisation hit me: this is my face, made of sticks that I smoked myself. It all began with a small box that didn't even hold fifty sticks, and now there were around 5,500 of them in front of me.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu8ssw5ssxmum5.jpg
content.caption: Self-portrait, 5,500 hand-painted sticks.
Self-portrait, details. Up close the face dissolves into separate shades.

content.content: One of your works refers to Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, a very recognisable image. What brought you to this portrait in particular, and did your relationship with it change while you were working on it?

I had liked Girl with a Pearl Earring for a long time. Back in Ukraine I painted my own version with a cat, and in Spain the image kept turning up everywhere. At some point I decided that she would be my first portrait made of sticks. A familiar image, familiar colours.
Before her I had made only two works from sticks, both abstract and with a fairly simple palette, so a portrait with so many shades was a big step for me.

When I finished the layout and realised how many shades and thousands of sticks I would have to paint by hand, I thought I had taken on too much. I even considered leaving it as elongated coloured pixels. It stayed in that state for quite a long time, until I finally talked myself into finishing what I'd started.
That is probably why I have a special love for this work. It was my first work on that scale, and the first that took me so long to complete, and in the end it became my favourite.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eqnywo8h9s9.jpg
content.caption: After Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, her first portrait made of sticks.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eqolect31v7.jpg
content.caption: Girl with a Pearl Earring, detail.

content.content: Besides mosaic, you work in oil painting, graphite studies and the series Elongated Pixels. Do you feel these languages as different voices in the same conversation, or does each one lead you somewhere else entirely?

In general I try not to divide my work into separate directions or tie everything together into one story. I simply like switching between different materials and techniques. I can finish a work in sticks, pick up watercolour or go back to oils, and then return to the sticks again.

Sometimes one thing grows directly out of another. Elongated Pixels, for example, were born while I was working on Girl with a Pearl Earring. At the layout stage I saw that the image looked interesting even without the sticks, and later I made Frida in this technique.
But it's still the sticks that I keep coming back to. Right now this is the material and the process I like most of all.
Among your works there is a canvas called La Guerra. I understand this may be a difficult subject, so I ask carefully: if you feel comfortable talking about it now, what stood behind this work?
For me this work is probably about the pain that stays inside because of the war. Life goes on, you do ordinary things, but it doesn't go away.
At first I wanted to leave hope in this work, the thought that after darkness light always comes. That was meant to be the sun. But in the process, instead of a ray of light, it began to bleed.
Even now I look at this work and feel everything tighten inside. For me, La Guerra is probably that very wound, the one that stays inside even when life around you goes on.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu2eqpcycqu7fm.jpg
content.caption: La Guerra.
La Guerra, details.

content.content: In 2026 your works were shown to the public for the first time at Russafa Art in Valencia. What was it like when people stood next to your mosaics and looked at them in person, rather than on a screen?

At Russafa Art I caught myself feeling a little out of place. There was a lot of painting around, and here I was with my used sticks. I felt awkward, and at the same time I was glad to finally be showing them, and afraid: how would people even take this?
The most interesting part was watching the reactions. Many people didn't understand what the works were made of. Some guessed pastel or chalk, but practically no one guessed used sticks.

The images themselves were also read in different ways. Girl with a Pearl Earring was recognised immediately, because almost everyone knows that image. The self-portrait was harder: people could look at it for a long time without understanding what was in front of them, but as soon as I showed them a photograph, the portrait became visible.

For me it was a very valuable experience. I saw live reactions to my work, received a lot of support and met new people. It's much easier for me to make works than to show them and talk about myself. Even keeping up with social media isn't easy for me, so taking part in Russafa Art was quite a big step. And I'm very grateful to everyone who supported me.
Allow me one last, slightly dreamy question: is there an image, a theme or a material you would like to take on one day, but for now lack the courage or the time?

One day I would like to try making a large-scale portrait out of much smaller elements. For now the complexity, the number of elements and the time it would take scare me a little. But once, a few thousand sticks also seemed far too complicated, and now with every new work the process becomes clearer and more precise for me.

In parallel I collect various materials that should have ended up in the rubbish but caught my attention for some reason. I don't know myself yet what they will become, or when. My ideas usually appear quite unexpectedly.

content.caption: In the studio with the portraits.

content.content: Photographs courtesy of Oksana Dzhuman. Interview conducted in writing for EPRIS Journal, September 2026.

articles.title: A Cow Made of Broken Tile
articles.author: Viacheslav Munister & DIHLUST
articles.excerpt: A family workshop on turning mosaic, a material invented never to move, into furniture that ships across oceans, and why a table with a cow on it is, they insist, mostly about the glass of milk you got after a day outside.

content.content: DIHLUST is a family workshop in Ukraine, run by a brother and sister who build small, cube shaped side tables entirely out of glazed mosaic tile. Every piece begins as a sketch reduced to a grid, most often a pixellated cow, their signature image, though a client's logo or a pet's portrait works just as well, then gets laid, tile by tile, onto a wooden frame built to carry the weight.

Their online listings read less like a shop and more like a missing-pet notice reworked for furniture: a promise that MILK-cube is “looking for a loving family.” Mosaic has meant permanence for two thousand years; DIHLUST packs it for international courier instead. EPRIS wrote to them with nine questions built around exactly that contradiction. They answered in their own words, translated here from Ukrainian and condensed for length.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/reidnol8cx8kzw.jpg

William Morris argued, a century and a half ago, that everyday objects deserve as much attention as painting, the idea the Arts and Crafts movement was built on. Tell us how DIHLUST began: why did a cube clad in mosaic, rather than a painting or a sculpture, become the object you chose to speak through?

The first reason is function. A side table is not a silent object, it is something we interact with every day: you set a coffee cup on it, put down a book or your keys. That means it can belong to any space, and it lives alongside our life. Marks get left on it, it gets used. It is a functional art object that erases the line between a certain high aesthetic and the everyday.

In Japanese folklore there is tsukumogami, the belief that an object, used long and carefully enough, eventually grows a soul of its own. Your listing “MILK-cube is looking for a loving family” says almost exactly that about furniture: factory objects are usually silent, yours seem to be looking for a home. Where does that impulse to humanise, or animalise, your own pieces come from? Do you genuinely feel each cube is a little alive, or is this mostly the language of marketing?

Of course there is a large part marketing in it, we like playing with concepts and metaphors. But every table really is unique, which makes it very easy to grow attached to it, almost like it is family.

The “loving family” listing is actually an old street form: a handwritten notice on a lamppost about a lost pet, with tear-off phone number strips along the bottom. You took that form almost literally and filled it with commercial content. What matters more to you in that gesture: irony about advertising, or a sincere attempt to make selling furniture feel as emotional as finding a home for an animal?

We carried that format over to furniture because every table of ours is unique. When you make something with your own hands, putting in tens of hours of work, it stops being just a product and takes on a character of its own, so we thought it would be great to build that into the piece in this style.

A cow and a glass of milk are a recurring motif in your work. Is that more a personal story from childhood or rural life, or a deliberate engagement with a pastoral, almost kolkhoz adjacent iconography that a lot of people in Ukraine right now either feel awkward about, or, on the contrary, are reclaiming with tenderness?

It is mainly about nostalgia. When we were thinking about which set to release first, as a family business, me and my brother, we wanted, for no particular reason, to start from where life itself starts: from childhood, from its warmest memories.

The image of a glass of milk is tied to something simple: how we would spend a whole summer day outside, running around, getting tired, and then that cold glass of milk felt like the tastiest thing in the world. Those are pure emotions and memories we wanted to put into our work. It seems like exactly the kind of nostalgic feeling that connects most people.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/jxr52jpm45561q.jpg

Mosaic has meant permanence for millennia: the floors of Byzantine churches, Gaudí's façades, things built to outlast generations in one place. You turn it into an object that can be lifted, embraced, sold and shipped across an ocean. What breaks in the idea of mosaic itself once it stops being part of a fixed space and becomes a thing that travels?
Nothing breaks. If anything, mosaic takes on an entirely new life here. We are not destroying its permanence, we are making it mobile. We are simply rethinking it.

Your profile has a “MEET OUR TEAM” family collage. Historically, a workshop where the whole family works is closer to a medieval guild, or to the early Eames Office, than to a contemporary design studio with hired staff. Was staying a family workshop a conscious choice, or did it simply happen that way because of scale?

It was a conscious choice, even though the whole thing was born spontaneously. We came up with the business itself in literally one day. Then we checked the market, realised nothing quite like this existed yet, and started acting right away.

Our family has always made things with our own hands: my brother paints and does plaster relief work on walls, our father can do a full renovation from scratch himself, so there was never really any doubt we could learn this too and build the picture we had in our heads. It is also a rare chance to do creative work that feeds the whole family at once, about as close to an ideal life scenario as it gets, because everything our family has ever had came through hard physical labour and a constant search for work.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/aw5t05llsrx3j7.jpg

Fragile tile on a wooden base, and yet worldwide shipping across oceans and customs: a material invented never to move again now has to survive a courier service. What did you actually have to change in your technique for the sake of the journey, rather than for the sake of beauty?

We had to make peace with the fact that packaging for each table ends up fairly expensive, around twenty to twenty-five percent of the table’s cost. That is a sacrifice we cannot show our work to the world without, so we just accepted it as a fact. We also had to reinforce the tables from the inside, which adds weight but is about durability. They weigh sixteen to thirty-one kilograms.

Your bio has the phrase “possible realisation of your own…”, meaning you are open to someone else’s idea. In a traditional craft guild the master usually carried out the patron's vision and kept his own voice hidden in the execution. Is it the same for you, or does the final word always stay with you while the client only sets the theme?

We are always interpreting someone else’s idea, but through the lens of our own style. All our tables stay pixellated and minimalist, but the image itself can be almost anything: a logo, a portrait of someone’s pet. The final word on style and form is always ours, because that is our artistic language, but the client sets the theme and the story. We get enormous pleasure from that process, watching a shared idea turn into a recognisable pixel art table.
