content.content: VM: That same project's brief was, as you put it, “wonderfully specific”: your clients had always dreamed of particular pieces from Italian design houses – a Poliform cabinet, a B&B Italia sofa, an Antonio Lupi basin – items you describe as “not simply items on a shopping list, but part of the image of the home they wanted to create.” When a client arrives already attached to the exact sofa and the exact basin, sometimes years before the room around those objects even exists, how do you design that room so it reads as something more than a frame built to justify a purchase already made?
OW: Each piece of furniture has its own history – of material, place of origin, style and suitability.

The furniture selected by the clients often told me more about the future interior than a conventional brief could. My task was to bring these individual objects into a conversation with the architecture, the views from the windows and one another, so that the interior would acquire a coherent language rather than become a collection of beautiful things.

For example, the black Poliform cabinet, designed by Piero Lissoni, led me towards black-veneered wall panels of the same architectural restraint. The colour of the B&B Italia sofa became the starting point for the bespoke kitchen, whose ceramic fronts were made in a closely related shade.

The clients had a particular affection for Italy, and I wanted to acknowledge that without making the house feel as though it belonged elsewhere. The Ukrainian landscape outside the windows remained essential. I brought its yellow and brown tones inside through yellowish terrazzo, travertine and the warm grey of Little Greene’s Slaked Lime – Dark 151. The garden partly obscured the view, which I came to see not as a limitation but as something that gave the sitting room a sense of intimacy – a room held gently between the house and nature.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotdefcyl80p.jpg
content.caption: The material board for Eight Years to a Home: terrazzo, travertine and the warm grey of Little Greene's Slaked Lime Dark 151.

content.content: 03 · The projects that wait

VM: Your house on the Fish Island has been listed as “In Progress” since 2020 – a 450-square-metre concrete-and-steel structure, envisioned explicitly as a prototype for several future houses to be built on the same riverbank, built around a client's very particular list: a swimming pool, a fish pond, dedicated parking for a car collection, and three bedrooms, one for each of his children. Six years is a long time for a prototype to still be a work in progress. Has the house itself changed across those six years – in brief, in detail, in what “prototype” even means for the houses that might follow it – or has the delay simply been the ordinary friction of building something this large?
OW: This is perhaps one of the more painful questions I might be asked.

The building project was cancelled when my clients lost the plot of land. There is something particularly difficult about seeing a house that has been carefully imagined never acquire the life for which it was intended.

And yet, the work did not entirely disappear. The concrete structure and its carefully resolved junctions found a second life in another house that was later conceived for the same site and exists there today.

Perhaps this is one of the quieter truths of architectural work: an idea does not always arrive at its first destination. Sometimes part of it survives, altered by circumstance, and continues its life somewhere else.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotdvmmcdg5v.jpg
content.caption: House on the Fish Island: the section cut through pool and terrace, the structure set into the hill.

content.content: VM: The Bridge House has the longest visible timeline in your entire portfolio – 2017 to 2026, described on your own site as an “evolution of the architectural concept” rather than a single continuous build. Its plan is organised as three distinct pieces: a single-level Forest Pavilion designed to nearly disappear into the landscape, a two-storey Main House built around an internal atrium for daylight and privacy, and the Bridge itself, which your notes call “more than a circulation element... the architectural symbol of the project.” Between “Eight Years to a Home,” the Fish Island house still listed as in progress since 2020, and now a nine-year evolution on the Bridge House – is this simply what building privately in Ukraine over the last decade has looked like for everyone in your position, or is a project that's allowed to evolve across many years actually closer to how you'd choose to work even without a war or a pandemic pushing the timeline?
OW: The Bridge House was first called The House Above an Old Road in 2017.
I do agree that, looking at it now, it appears almost as a bridge between my past career and the work I do today.

Much of what I had learned through my years of working in the Netherlands and the UK found its place in this house. But its story is not only about a timeline. There was another, more personal connection: my client had lived and studied in the Netherlands for many years.
In a way, the materials became the language through which the three of us – the architect, the house and the client – were connected to that place.
We chose MIB GeoStylistix facing bricks, concrete junctions inspired by the House on the Fish Island, and Alpi veneer, which I had first discovered in Amsterdam.

Perhaps this is why the house has always felt to me like more than a project. It carries pieces of places, experience and memory from different periods of my life, brought together in one piece of architecture.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotea15zlq4v.jpg
content.caption: Bridge House: the Forest Pavilion, shaped around the trees that were kept rather than cleared.

content.content: 04 · Unbuilt, and still alive

VM: In Tuscany, you sketched an extension – 2024 – for what your own project notes describe as a “1 Euro House”: one of the abandoned homes Italian municipalities sell for a symbolic euro to buyers who commit to restoring them, in towns trying to survive depopulation. Your plan called for selectively demolishing the existing structure, removing an intermediate floor to create a double-height space, and building a new balcony to connect the old house to a new 60-square-metre extension. What drew you personally to a project built on a premise so different from the rest of your portfolio – not a client with an unlimited wish-list, but a near-abandoned building in a town that is, in its own way, asking to be saved?

OW: It was a precious time to learn and to create a house for my friends from Israel. It was a voluntary project, but it gave me something I needed very much that summer in Kyiv in 2023: a reason to create, and a way to survive the summer emotionally.

Kate, the daughter of my friend, was already dreaming of her future adult life in Italy. So I began to imagine the extension almost as a doll’s house for that future life – a small world of her own, rather than simply an addition to the existing house. Her mother sent me the brief and the possible site, and I began to write a story for the future.

I studied the village from a distance, learning its details online and reading the structure of the surrounding landscape through Google Maps. I was also inspired by the quiet architecture of contemporary Tuscan wineries – their relationship with the land, their simplicity, and the feeling that the building had always belonged there.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucoteq6vnbj1k.jpg
content.caption: TOSCANA HOUSE: the proposed extension to a one euro house, glazed towards the valley.

content.content: VM: “House near the Dam” is a 2019 sketch, never (as far as your portfolio shows) built: two connected volumes in Kyiv's Dam District, clad in red brick and wood to match the surrounding red pines, with a sloped roof planted with wild herbs specifically so the house would blend into the meadow rather than announce itself from the road. A living roof is a very particular kind of promise – it asks a client to accept years of upkeep for the sake of near-invisibility. What usually happens to a design like this one, that asks that much commitment for that much restraint – does it stay unbuilt because the ambition was too specific for the client who eventually came along, or because the right site and the right client for it simply haven't met yet?

OW: The house remained a sketch, as the client eventually relocated to the UK as a Ukrainian refugee. The land is still waiting for them, and the sketch – something we were both rather proud of – still exists.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojr5smt4w9p.jpg
content.caption: House near the Dam: timber and brick among the red pines of Kyiv's Dam District.

content.content: 05 · A restaurant, a studio, a penthouse

VM: CICADA, your restaurant and wine bar project from 2018, came with an unusual condition attached to the brief itself: the client – who had researched the restaurant industry extensively through travel across Europe and Australia – specifically wanted an architect with no previous experience designing restaurants, precisely so the process could stay collaborative and the ideas could stay unconventional. The restaurant's chef, meanwhile, had circled the world three times gathering inspiration for a genuinely multicultural menu. What does it actually feel like to be hired because you're inexperienced in a category, rather than in spite of it – and did that freedom from precedent change how boldly you were willing to work, on a project that went on to be featured in ATTITUDE Magazine?

OW: I had spent many years visiting restaurants across Europe and the UK, observing not only how they looked, but how they made one feel, how people moved through them, and how a room could shape an evening.

My work was always rooted in the client’s brief, but I have never been very interested in clichés about what a restaurant is supposed to be. I wanted to understand how this particular one might live, and then allow the idea to take its own shape.

The entire project was carried out online. We spoke with builders and contractors through a screen; samples of materials travelled to me in Kyiv. At the time, it felt almost audacious to imagine that everything could be created this way – a restaurant existing, for a while, between a distant site and a desk in Kyiv.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojsdijslkdx.jpg
content.caption: CICADA restaurant and wine bar, designed entirely through a screen from a desk in Kyiv.

content.content: VM: You also designed the office for your own practice, Olga Akulova DESIGN – completed in 2010, photographed once that year and again six years later in 2016, and highly commended at the International Property Awards in London in 2012. That's the one project in your portfolio with no outside client to negotiate against, argue with, or ultimately answer to. Looking back at a space you designed entirely for yourself, and that still held up well enough to be re-photographed six years on – what did you learn about your own taste when there was no one else's taste to balance it against, and is there anything in that office you would design differently today?
OW: I designed my studio in three days. Perhaps because it was my own space, there was no need to explain the idea to anyone before making it happen.

Fourteen years later, I am restyling the interior as I continue to grow as an architect. New materials have appeared, new technologies have changed what is possible, and I have found a colour for the walls that feels more right now – Rolling Fog by Little Greene.

And yet the room still draws me back to Kyiv. There is the view of the garden, my own little England; the Boffi K4, around which the kitchen was shaped; and the wooden floor, which has aged beautifully over these fourteen years.

All this time, the studio has also been a kind of working catalogue of my practice. It is where I have met clients, and where they could see, rather than simply hear me describe, the junctions, materials and language of the interiors I make.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojsxsvru3jf.jpg
content.caption: A sectional study from the studio's working drawings.

content.content: VM: Your NPL Penthouse – the 30th floor of the Novopecherskie Lipki condominium in Kyiv, bought by your client purely as an investment property – came with a brief that was really an absence of a brief: exposed concrete ceilings, full-height glass, and then almost total silence, because the client had “limited time to be involved” and asked you to complete the entire interior and fit-out independently. The project went on to be featured in Dezeen, Moroso and Leibal. When a client effectively hands you the keys and steps back entirely, is that the freest you ever get to work, or does an absent client's silence create its own, quieter kind of pressure that a demanding one never would?

OW: Exactly. The pressure created by the absence of a client was enormous. To prove to myself that I was worthy of making the project without a client’s editorial hand, I brought everything I knew at that time to it, and pushed my knowledge and possibilities as far as I could.

My travels to the UK became an important part of the process. I bought some of the accessories for the penthouse in London, at the Designers Guild showroom, and the poster for the kitchen in London as well. They were not souvenirs of a journey, but things that had already found their place in the project in my mind.
My contractors worked with remarkable precision and care, following the project closely. And, eventually, the penthouse travelled further than any of us had imagined – into worldwide publications.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojt7bapt3de.jpg
content.caption: NPL Penthouse, thirtieth floor of Novopecherskie Lipki in Kyiv: exposed concrete, full height glass and oak joinery.

content.content: 06 · Method and motifs

VM: A project titled simply “House near the Dam” is filed in your portfolio under the single word “minimalism” – a word that can mean an empty room just as easily as it can mean a room where every remaining object had to earn, and fight for, the right to stay. When you strip a house down that far for a real client with a real life to live inside it, what is your actual working method for deciding what earns that right – and has a client ever fought you to keep something you were certain had to go?

OW: When my clients are unsure about a particular piece of furniture or an item in the project, I first try to understand what lies behind their hesitation. It may be the budget, a style they have not mentioned in the brief, or simply that my idea is more daring than they had imagined for themselves.

When we discuss a possible change, I look for something that answers their concern without disturbing the composition that already exists. The new piece still has to belong to the whole, and, most importantly, to my client at that particular moment.
That is part of the work: not persuading a client to accept my idea, but understanding when an idea needs to change – and when it simply needs to be explained.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotf5wvs8qek.jpg
content.caption: An attic bedroom in progress: the point where a minimal room decides what stays.

content.content: VM: Several of your project titles read less like catalogue entries and more like private diary lines – “With a dream of KENZO,” “Uplifted House,” “Interior for Kate & Corgis” – the kind of phrase that usually stays inside a client's head, not on a public portfolio page. Where do these titles actually come from: are they yours, coined out of how the project felt to live through as its designer, or do they belong to the clients – a private joke, a private hope, a pet's name – that somehow made it, intact and unedited, all the way into your public-facing work?
OW: You made me smile.

I live through each project, and its name usually comes to me as a result of the work rather than at the beginning. It is almost a conclusion – the main idea that has slowly shaped the project through months, sometimes years, of working together.

Each project becomes a story in its own right. We see it afterwards in photographs, but my clients continue to live inside it. Perhaps that is why the name appears only when the story has already revealed itself.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojun09ei7x3.jpg
content.caption: One of the Kyiv interiors whose name arrived only once the project was finished.

content.content: VM: Looking at your Bridge House concept specifically – a pavilion designed to vanish into a pine forest, connected by a bridge you call the project's “architectural symbol” to a house organised around an internal garden bringing light into its own centre – how literally do you take the idea of a threshold in your work generally? Is the bridge, the terrace, the balcony that keeps recurring across your projects (the terrace in “Eight Years to a Home,” the balcony in TOSCANA HOUSE, the riverside terrace on Fish Island) a functional feature you return to because clients keep asking for it, or is it the closest thing your work has to a genuine, recurring architectural signature?
OW: Bridge House.
The shape was created by the existing trees. We cherished them, rather than asking them to give way to the house.
The Eight Years to a Home.
The garden – nature itself – is the element that connects all my projects.
Toscana House.
The roof terrace and balcony were conceived as a way of bringing the house towards the mountain view.
Fish Island House.
The terrace is set into the hill to find the best possible view of the water on the site.
Perhaps this is what I could call my architectural signature: I always try to connect my clients with nature. It is the most inseparable relationship a house can have.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotfjf3mxutj.jpg
content.caption: The sitting room opening onto the terrace: the threshold Olha Wood calls her architectural signature.

content.content: 07 · Distance, and what it costs

VM: Your work now moves between Kyiv, Denmark, and clients across the UK, frequently without you standing physically inside the rooms you're shaping until very late in the process, if at all – site visits replaced by video calls, timber and stone chosen from photographs and swatches sent by courier rather than held in your own hand. Materials like your namesake wood are famously about grain, weight, and how light actually falls across a surface in person. What does an interior architect concretely lose when a project has to be built at that kind of distance – and is there anything, unexpectedly, that the distance makes easier, clearer, or even better?
OW: Strong communication with clients – video calls, being in regular contact, friendship and empathy – can create a surprisingly close connection with a building site, even from a long distance.

Materials are now available across countries, too. And after 25 years of experience, I know how to find the right ones, work with people locally, and keep the architectural idea consistent, wherever the site may be.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucojvm6r3rgi5.jpg
content.caption: Site and finished room side by side, the process Olha Wood now follows at a distance.

content.content: VM: “Eight years to a Home” ends, in your own account, in August 2026 – the work “very close to the end” – in a Kyiv that is still, as you're answering this, a city living through war. When you finally hand your clients the keys to a home eight years, one pandemic, and one full-scale war in the making, what do you think that specific moment will actually feel like, for them and for you – and is it a feeling any earlier, easier project in your portfolio could possibly have prepared you for?
OW: The building site is still ongoing. In Kyiv, we do not have an abundance of contractors at the moment, as many of them are protecting our country.
We hope to complete part of the work this autumn. My clients can hardly wait to begin their life in the space they have dreamed of for so many years.

The garden, which was completed on the terrace a year ago, has already given them something to live with while the house is still being made. They have spent this time among the greenery, watching it grow, and hoping that soon their life in the house will begin.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mucotfyucooqvn.jpg
content.caption: The terrace garden at Eight Years to a Home, completed a year before the house it belongs to.

content.content: VM: You've now spent years designing homes for people staying in a country at war, for an apartment building's shared future on an island, for a nearly abandoned house in a depopulating Italian town, and for landscapes – a stream, a pine grove, a riverbank – that were there long before any client and will presumably outlast the buildings too. If a future client asked you to design something with no constraints at all – no budget ceiling, no site, no deadline – what is the one idea sitting somewhere in your unbuilt sketches, the Tuscany extension or the Dam District house or something you haven't shown anyone yet, that you would actually choose to build first?
OW: It would be wonderful to allow myself to dream about a future project.
Perhaps it would be a house in the UK – an extension to an old house at the end of a quiet road, in the forest, with a hill and a meadow opening towards the trees.
I imagine a studio for work attached to the main house, and a terrace at the top of the hill, looking across the meadow towards the forest.

Wood, glass and local stone. A house that belongs to its place rather than simply occupying it. Sustainable and energy-independent, but without making sustainability the aesthetic. It would simply be part of the way the house lives.

reviews.title: Dinner Inside an Advertisement
reviews.subject: Le Train Bleu · Gare de Lyon, Paris · Marius Toudoire
reviews.author: Viacheslav Munister
reviews.meta: PARIS · MARIUS TOUDOIRE · 1900–1901 · MONUMENT HISTORIQUE 1972 · PHOTO: CC0 / WIKIMEDIA COMMONS
reviews.verdict: Le Train Bleu does not serve nostalgia. It serves a hundred-and-twenty-five-year-old sales pitch for a train that stopped running in 2003, inside a room the French state has legally frozen since 1972 — and asks you to pay, gladly, for the privilege of hearing it again.
pros: Forty-one paintings by seventeen artists turn the dining room into a functioning 1900 travel advertisement, not mere decoration
Monument Historique status (1972) has kept the 2014 restoration disciplined — nothing modernised that didn't need to be
The menu (Michel Rostang since 2018) plays a supporting role rather than reinterpreting the room, which is the right call inside a monument
Rare case of a piece of purely commercial, corporate architecture — built by a railway company to sell tickets — preserved with the same rigor as a cathedral
cons: The kitchen's deliberate old-fashioned register (lamb from the trolley, tableside tartare) will read as expensive nostalgia rather than cuisine to some diners
As a working station buffet inside an active terminus, the room trades some quiet for constant foot traffic and tourist volume

content.content: Climb the double staircase at the Gare de Lyon and you leave the railway. Below, the platforms run on schedules measured in minutes; the trains themselves have changed shape four or five times since the building opened. Above, nothing has been allowed to change at all. You are standing inside a room built in 1900 to sell a train that no longer exists, for a company that no longer exists, to a public that has been dead for a century. The room outlived all three. It is called Le Train Bleu, it is a working restaurant with a wine list and a reservations line, and since 1972 it has also been a Monument Historique of France - a piece of advertising copy that the state now protects the way it protects cathedrals.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mton40n3v6m216.jpg
content.alt: Period postcard of the monumental staircase inside the Gare de Lyon, leading up to the station buffet, early twentieth century
content.caption: The staircase to the Buffet de la Gare de Lyon, photographed not long after it opened. The restaurant now called Le Train Bleu sits at the top of it.

content.content: A brochure you can sit inside

The commission was never really for a restaurant. In 1900 the Compagnie des chemins de fer de Paris à Lyon et à la Méditerranée - the PLM - was rebuilding its Paris terminus from scratch for the Exposition Universelle, and it needed the new station to do more than move passengers through a building. It needed to convince them to keep coming back for a destination most of them had never seen: Provence, the Riviera, Algiers. The architect Marius Toudoire, who had already drawn the station's facade and its 67-metre clock tower, built in open homage to Big Ben, was asked to build a dining room that would do the selling. He built a room 26 metres long with a ceiling that behaves like a painted sky, and he covered its walls in forty-one paintings by seventeen different artists - Albert Maignan, Henri Gervex, François Flameng, Eugène Burnand among them - each one an advertisement for a city the trains below were supposed to reach. Orange, Marseille, Nice, Monaco, Algiers: you could eat your dinner and plan your whole itinerary off the walls without ever consulting a timetable.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mton40ylg933pv.jpg
content.alt: Detail of a Belle Epoque mural inside Le Train Bleu, signed Albert Maignan 1905, depicting a garden party above the Roman theatre at Orange
content.caption: One of the forty-one wall paintings, signed by Albert Maignan and dated 1905, labelled simply Orange - a stop on the PLM line rendered as a scene from high society rather than a photograph of a station.
content.credit: Photo: Mbzt / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0

content.content: This is worth pausing on, because it is easy to file the room under “ornate” and move on to the food. A photograph documents a place. A commissioned oil painting, forty of them, hung at the scale of a cathedral, does something closer to a pitch: it tells you what the place feels like to the people who can afford to be there, which is a different and much more persuasive claim. The PLM was not decorating a waiting room. It was building the nineteenth century's version of a full-page spread in a glossy magazine, except the spread was eleven metres tall, gilded, lit by bronze chandeliers, and structurally load-bearing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mton41e22lwc01.jpg
content.alt: Gilded stucco ceiling of Le Train Bleu with a bronze chandelier in the foreground and painted medallions labelled Paris and Lyon
content.caption: The ceiling of the Grande Salle: painted city medallions set into stucco scrollwork, lit by the original bronze chandeliers.

content.content: The measurements of an illusion

The room has a name for every part of the fiction. The Salle Dorée, the Golden Room, runs 18.5 metres long under an 11-metre ceiling. The main dining room carries the name Réjane, after the actress who was one of its first regulars. Off to one side, the Salons Tunisien and Algérien - carved dark wood, geometric Arab motifs, orientalist landscapes - were built to stage a version of French Algeria for businessmen who would never travel there, favourite rooms for lunch meetings for exactly that reason. None of these spaces pretend to be modest. The building's decoration budget alone, in 1900 francs, could have built a provincial train station of its own. That was, in a sense, the point: the PLM was competing with rival railway companies for the same wealthy passengers, and the fastest way to prove your trains were worth taking was to prove your waiting room was worth living in.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mton41s025cv5t.jpg
content.alt: Sculpted plaque above an archway in Le Train Bleu recording that President Emile Loubet inaugurated the buffet on 7 April 1901, flanked by two carved mermaids
content.caption: The dedication still on the wall: “Emile Loubet, Président de la République Française, inaugura ce buffet le VII avril MDCCCCI.” The head of state opened a train station restaurant the way other governments open bridges.

content.content: President Emile Loubet cut the ribbon himself on 7 April 1901, a detail the room still advertises on a carved plaque flanked by two mermaids, as if the opening of a station buffet required the same ceremony as a war memorial. In its first decades the room was simply called the Buffet de la Gare de Lyon - a functional name for a functional-sounding job, dining hall attached to a station. It only became Le Train Bleu in 1963, and this is where the story gets stranger rather than simpler: the overnight express it renamed itself after, with its dark-blue sleeping cars running between Calais and the Riviera, was still in service at the time - it would keep running for another forty years, until 2003. But by 1963 jet travel had already taken the glamour the train used to own; the Riviera was now a few hours away by air, and the twenty-hour sleeper had quietly slid from the fastest way to arrive into the most romantic way to be delayed. The restaurant borrowed the name at exactly the moment the real train stopped being the point and started being the legend. It has been selling a memory of travel since before the thing it named itself after had finished happening.
A monument that keeps serving lunch

In 1972 the French state made that memory official, listing the restaurant, the Salle Dorée, and the Tunisian and Algerian salons as Monuments Historiques - the same designation that protects Notre-Dame and the châteaux of the Loire. It is an unusual thing to protect: not a ruin, not a museum piece behind rope barriers, but a functioning commercial dining room that still needs working kitchens, fire exits, and a wine cellar. The paradox produced its own discipline. When the restaurant closed for three months in the summer of 2014 for a 4.5 million euro restoration - cleaning and repairing all forty-one paintings, regilding the stucco, rewiring chandeliers that had been retrofitted for electricity a century earlier - the work was led jointly by Agence Duthilleul, the practice responsible for the TGV network's stations, and an Architecte des Monuments Historiques, whose job was to make sure modernity touched nothing anyone could see. Architect Jean-Marie Duthilleul described the building's original idea as a doorway to the Mediterranean set inside Paris, its departing trains staged like ships leaving for somewhere exotic. The 2014 renovation restored that idea rather than updating it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mton3zskryhe6c.jpg
content.alt: Wide interior view of Le Train Bleu, showing the gilded oval bar counter, painted barrel-vaulted ceiling, chandeliers, and diners at white-clothed tables
content.caption: The Grande Salle Réjane, 26 metres of painted ceiling over a room that has not stopped serving dinner since 1901.

content.content: What survived the century is not only plaster. The room absorbed a cultural afterlife it was never built to expect. Coco Chanel and Jean Cocteau took tables there in the 1920s; Colette wrote about it; Salvador Dalí, Brigitte Bardot and Jean Gabin were regulars later on. Seven films have used it as a location, from Travels with My Aunt in 1972 to the Mr. Bean holiday comedy in 2007 - a Belle Époque dining room playing itself, decade after decade, in stories that had nothing to do with railways. Each generation found a slightly different fiction to project onto the same forty-one paintings. That is what a genuinely successful piece of advertising does: it stops needing the product it was built to sell, and starts selling the feeling of having always been there.
What is actually on the table

None of this would matter if the kitchen had modernised to match the ambition of the room, and to its credit it never has. Since 2018 the restaurant has been run for its operator, SSP, by the chef Michel Rostang, and the menu he built is deliberately unfashionable: leg of lamb carved tableside from a trolley, a gratin dauphinois made without cheese or egg in the old style, Bresse chicken with tarragon cream, steak tartare mixed in front of you, rum baba finished with a pour of rum at the table. There is no attempt to reinterpret the room in the kitchen's own image, the way a contemporary chef might feel obliged to do inside a monument. The food plays the same supporting role the paintings do: proof that a version of France existing mostly in memory is, for the length of a meal, still available to order.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mton426yr3s0w9.jpg
content.alt: Daytime exterior of the Gare de Lyon facade, with arched windows carrying oval signs reading Le Train Bleu, above the station's entrance canopies
content.caption: The station facade Toudoire designed alongside the restaurant, its arched windows still carrying the restaurant's name to the square outside.
content.credit: Photo: APB11 / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content.content: Downstairs, the trains that made the room's fortune have mostly moved on. The line to the Riviera runs faster now and stops less; the TGV that eventually replaced the original Train Bleu does not carry its name, and passengers who want the coast today are more likely to compare fares on a phone than to sit down in a dining room and be sold the destination in oil paint. The advertisement, in other words, has completely outlived the product. What is left is a room that no longer has to persuade anyone of anything, protected by law from ever having to try a different pitch, still setting a table under a ceiling built to make you believe a train ride could feel like arriving somewhere before you had left. Eat there and you are not visiting the past. You are sitting inside a hundred-and-twenty-five-year-old sales pitch that the French state decided was worth telling forever, and paying, gladly, for the privilege of hearing it again.

reviews.title: Le Dauphine
reviews.subject: 131 Avenue Parmentier, Paris

content.content: Quality bistronomy. Le Dauphine, located in the 11th arrondissement of Paris, is an exposed, rather than a hidden gem of the city. Thanks to the architects Rem Koolhaas and Clément Blanchet, who worked on the restoration of the dining space, the entrance of the shiny and tiny restaurant features a massive white frame, embracing the glass facade and providing an open view of the magnificent interior.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbpdtwm8fm1zc.webp

The duo of star chefs – Fred Péneau and Inaki Aizpitarte – commissioned the OMA bureau and Clément Blanchet to transform less than 60 square meters into a quality bistro-gastronomy space. In 2010, Le Dauphine opened its doors, immediately gaining the attention and love of the public, both for its design and cuisine.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbpfodp7mc2k6.webp

Surprisingly, the architects saw the place through the lens of an ancient temple – characterized by strong hierarchy and functions, which were borrowed and delicately implemented. The Naos is typified by the central bar counter – the heart of the space, covered in oak wood. Four encircled pillars amplify its relation to the ancient temple. The central counter is the heart, whose warmth contrasts with the total marble covering of the walls. The material usually associated with bathrooms defies the conventions of dining interiors and accomplishes it with great success. The whole space – from ceiling to floor – is laid in large-scale stone slabs with restrained graphic veins. Simplistic but chic – that’s a perfect background for a tasteful lunch on the rush, or an unhurried dinner, when the Parisian street lights transmute the exterior into an homage to one of Edouard Leon Cortes’s paintings.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbpw1txo5dnn1.webp
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbpjad387xo0q.webp

The exterior frame, described in the beginning, continues the storyline of the Hellenistic Sanctuary with due honor. Serving as the transition between the exalted interior and the street, it contains the magic of an immersive experience. To stop from the mundane to the sanctuary of tastes – where every deliberate choice elevates your experience of quality – is to reinterpret the classical pronaos, separating the external world from the sacral.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbpuvht9d8y4o.webp

Despite the modest area, the restaurant doesn’t feel compressed – the walls are not perceived restrictively by virtue of mirror panels reflecting the bright marble, tables, and happy guests who share the delight of being in a modern urban sanctuary.
The most distinctive element adopted from the Hellenistic Temple is the feeling of monumentality – the interior exudes a solid confidence in its own independence of time and trends.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbptvabvc2ngx.webp

It has proven to be true – 16 years after its opening in 2010, you can still visit Le Dauphine and join the joy at the center counter on a bar stool, or reserve a table for a cozy, modern bohemian dinner with your closest one.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msbpxbq4cbdynt.webp

reviews.title: Dining Inside a Watercolour
reviews.subject: Enigma · Barcelona · RCR Arquitectes

content.content: Enigma does not greet you with a grand dining room. It begins with a shimmer, a blurred silhouette and the feeling that something is being held back. RCR Arquitectes and Pau Llimona designed Albert Adrià’s Barcelona restaurant as a sequence of discoveries rather than a single interior: thresholds, veils and changing light postpone the moment when the whole place can be understood. The 514.78-square-metre project was designed in 2014–15 and built in 2015–16, yet its defining material is not glass, stone or steel. It is an RCR watercolour, enlarged and translated across ceramic floors, walls and furniture until a drawing becomes a place.

That translation is the key to Enigma’s identity. A more conventional restaurant might repeat a logo, a signature colour or one photogenic motif. Here identity behaves like weather: it surrounds the guest without turning into signage. Pale mineral surfaces erase hard edges; ribbed glass makes neighbouring tables present but unreadable; suspended forms lower and expand the ceiling without announcing themselves as sculpture. Nothing shouts “brand”, yet everything feels unmistakably related.

This is not neutral hospitality design. The route choreographs anticipation, exposure and retreat. A guest moves through the restaurant as a reader moves through paragraphs – never seeing the conclusion too soon. The meal can therefore change tempo without fighting the room. Seasonal cooking and spatial sequence share the same principle: meaning accumulates through succession.

There is a risk. Enigma’s visual language is so total that it can feel almost clinically controlled, and anyone looking for the informal warmth of Barcelona may read its translucent boundaries as distance. Yet the discipline is also the project’s achievement. RCR does not decorate Adrià’s food. It constructs the perceptual conditions in which surprise remains possible.

The result is rare: an interior with a recognisable image but no single photogenic trick. Enigma is strongest not when photographed, but when crossed. Its real luxury is not marble, privacy or spectacle. It is the careful design of attention.
A room drawn before it was built

The project began with a wash of pigment rather than a catalogue of finishes. RCR’s watercolour was enlarged, digitised and translated into a ceramic system that crosses floors, walls and custom furniture. At close range the surfaces are precise and manufactured; from a few metres away they lose their edges and behave like an atmospheric field. That tension – industrial control producing visual uncertainty – is the interior’s central idea. It also explains why the restaurant resists the usual hierarchy of feature wall, decorative ceiling and statement object: each plane belongs to the same continuous drawing.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msu3sr0ky3ccqx.webp
content.caption: The watercolour translated into a continuous interior field. Photo: Hisao Suzuki / RCR Arquitectes.

content.content: The photographs reveal how little of the room can be described by a single material name. Cast glass reads alternately as curtain, ice, rain and polished stone. Pale tables and chairs almost disappear into the reflective ground, while darker service elements collect in recesses. Instead of using contrast to clarify circulation, RCR uses degrees of opacity. Movement is guided by what remains partly visible: a glint of stainless steel, a silhouette behind ribbed glass, a warmer pocket of light beyond the next partition.
Identity without a logo

Enigma’s strongest branding decision is to avoid looking branded. The visual system is built from behaviours rather than emblems: translucency instead of a fixed graphic mark, repetition without perfect sameness, cool grey surfaces interrupted by warmer light, and a route that reveals information gradually. The watercolour supplies a recognisable texture, but the deeper identity lies in how the room acts. It filters, delays, reflects and reframes. The restaurant can therefore remain coherent across architecture, furniture and table setting without reducing itself to a colour palette. This is spatial identity at its most convincing: guests may forget an individual detail, but they remember the sensation of moving through the whole.
Thresholds, veils and withheld views
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msu3tifa1gj342.webp
content.caption: Ribbed glass filters movement and turns adjacent rooms into shifting silhouettes. Photo: Hisao Suzuki / RCR Arquitectes.

content.content: Enigma is organised as a sequence of perceptual edits. Screens interrupt long views without sealing rooms; compressed passages release into wider dining zones; ceiling formations seem to descend, then dissolve. The route never offers the conventional restaurant reveal in which reception gives way to one comprehensible dining room. Each transition withholds the next scene, turning circulation into part of the tasting menu. This is architecture performing the same work as a course: isolating an encounter, controlling its duration and leaving a residue before the next begins.
The kitchen as part of the architecture
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msu3tk8wazokbl.webp
content.caption: Service and dining zones share the same mineral, translucent language. Photo: Hisao Suzuki / RCR Arquitectes.

content.content: The open work areas are not presented as theatrical stages with chefs under spotlights. They are folded into the same silver-grey landscape as the dining room. Equipment, counters and storage appear through translucent layers, close enough to register as activity but abstracted enough to preserve concentration. This is an unusually intelligent answer to the open-kitchen cliché. Labour is neither hidden nor converted into spectacle; it becomes a changing depth behind the meal. Sound, reflection and movement make the kitchen present even when its exact boundaries remain uncertain.
Eating as a form of editing

The original Enigma did not merely serve a long menu in an unusual room; it cut the evening into scenes. Contemporary accounts described guests moving through a Welcome Area, wine cellar, cocktail bar, open kitchens, grill and extended dining room before ending in a darker final bar. Thirty-five to forty small dishes became a sequence of spatial cuts: stand, taste, move, sit, watch, wait. The most interesting connection between Adrià and RCR is therefore not “experimental food in experimental architecture”. It is their shared use of editing. Both remove context, isolate an encounter and then rearrange the order in which meaning arrives. A translucent wall performs the architectural equivalent of a covered plate: it tells you something is close while refusing to reveal it yet.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msu586ou220kra.jpg
content.caption: A course isolated against white space turns plating into a pause in the sequence. Official image: Enigma Barcelona.

content.content: An identity designed to mutate

The restaurant has since changed course. Enigma’s own current presentation says that little remains of the earlier format after reopening; today the tasting menu is rebuilt month by month around seasonal products and may run to roughly twenty to twenty-five dishes. That evolution makes the original identity strategy look even smarter. A logo-led concept would date the moment the menu changed. RCR’s system is more elastic because it is based on sensations – blur, reflection, anticipation, coolness, release. The cooking can be rewritten while the central promise remains legible: you enter a world where the familiar is made temporarily strange. In brand terms, Enigma owns a mode of attention rather than a decorative style.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msu586j2dklqit.jpg
content.caption: The dining room beneath its cloudlike ceiling: furniture, light and reflection merge into one field. Official image: Enigma Barcelona / Davide Groppi.

content.content: Barcelona without the postcard

There are no terracotta walls, market graphics or easy quotations of Mediterranean colour. Enigma belongs to Barcelona by refusing the postcard version of Barcelona. Its local character is carried more subtly: the culture of radical hospitality experiments associated with the Adrià orbit; RCR’s Catalan habit of treating material, landscape and ritual as one problem; and a confidence that craft can look futuristic without becoming anonymous. The restaurant’s official description calls the space both local and universal. That apparent contradiction is accurate. The project is rooted in a specific experimental culture, yet it communicates through basic bodily experiences – approaching, glimpsing, touching, waiting – that need no translation.
Why the space still matters
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/msu3tm0wqfgerp.webp
content.caption: Light changes the apparent depth and weight of every surface. Photo: Hisao Suzuki / RCR Arquitectes.

content.content: Years after completion, Enigma remains persuasive because its concept is not a styling package. The interior establishes rules – continuous image, filtered visibility, choreographed sequence – and allows every detail to follow them. The result can feel cool and exacting, but that coolness is productive: it clears away the visual noise that usually competes with ambitious food. RCR and Llimona created a restaurant that cannot be reduced to a photogenic corner. Its architecture is experienced cumulatively, through steps, pauses, reflections and partial views. The building does not explain the menu; it teaches the guest how to pay attention.

reviews.author: Viacheslav Munister
reviews.verdict: Enigma does not decorate a dinner. It gives the evening its own visual grammar – and asks the guest to read it one room at a time.
pros: Architecture choreographs the meal without becoming scenery
A watercolour becomes a coherent and adaptable identity system
Light, translucency and thresholds control pace with exceptional precision
The spatial concept remains meaningful even as the restaurant format evolves
cons: Its total visual control can feel emotionally cool
The experience depends on surrendering to a highly directed sequence

reviews.title: Marrow Deep
reviews.subject: Mastodon · Loma Vista Recordings · 2026
reviews.author: Viacheslav Munister
reviews.verdict: Marrow Deep does not mourn quietly. It erects a structure large enough to hold grief, and then challenges you to walk through each of its rooms.
pros: The five-song suite centered on Out Like a Lamb turns the epitaph into architecture, not spectacle.
New members Nick Johnston and João Nogueira are integrated into the band’s sound, rather than announced through it.
Golden Spires is built in literally ascending steps and earns the title.
cons: Across its thirteen tracks, the album occasionally repeats a form it has already proven it can build.
The album urges you to read it as a continuous structure, offering no single transitional moment for those seeking one.

content.content: Marrow Deep, released on August 28, 2026, is the first Mastodon album made without Brent Hinds, who left the band in March 2025 and died five months later in a motorcycle accident. The cover does not name this loss, but every review still reads the album through him, and so does this one: a band rebuilding publicly, with two new permanent members, guitarist Nick Johnston and keyboardist João Nogueira, who are integrated into the sound rather than announced by it.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mtojbvohbhfu1j.jpg
content.caption: Mastodon live at Rock im Park, 2022. Photo: Mr. Rossi, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

content.content: What holds the thirteen tracks together is less a theme than a construction method. Critics have already employed cathedral-like language to describe it: a song that winds upward like a snake, raises a tower, and combines towers, transepts, and buttresses as it ascends. Golden Spires earns its title under these conditions. It builds not so much toward a chorus as toward a ceiling, verse stacked on verse, until a coda appears like a vault closing overhead. This is an album that thinks in sections and heights, not just in riffs.

The emotional heart of the album is a five‑song suite that begins with Out Like a Lamb, the eulogy by drummer and singer Brann Dailor for his mother, whose title is borrowed from the old proverb about March weather. It is the quietest structural gesture on the album, with the bass moving beneath the vocals rather than behind them, and it lays out the foundation on which the rest of the suite is built.

With thirteen titles, Marrow Deep occasionally repeats a form it has already proven it can build, and an album that is so designed to be read as a continuous structure will frustrate anyone looking for a single crossover moment. It offers none. What it instead offers is a band that chooses architecture over spectacle to carry something so heavy, and mostly succeeds.

reviews.title: The Restaurant That Painted an 18th-Century House Pink
reviews.subject: sketch, The Gallery · 9 Conduit Street, Mayfair, London · India Mahdavi
reviews.author: Viacheslav Munister
reviews.meta: LONDON · INDIA MAHDAVI, DAVID SHRIGLEY · 1779 / 2014 · PHOTO: FLODEAU
reviews.verdict: Sketch takes a Grade II listed Georgian townhouse built by James Wyatt in 1779 and paints one of its rooms the exact pink of a 1980s prom dress, hangs two hundred and thirty-nine David Shrigley drawings on the walls in a grid, and puts a rainbow-lit chamber of egg-shaped toilet pods one floor below it, and asks diners to move between all three without once explaining the joke.
pros: The Gallery's monochrome pink scheme by India Mahdavi covers walls, banquettes, carpet and lighting in one continuous hue rather than treating pink as an accent, which is what makes the room read as a single artwork instead of a themed dining room

David Shrigley's 239 drawings are hung salon-style, uniformly framed and gridded across every wall, so the deliberately childish, deadpan sketches read as wallpaper from across the room and as individual jokes up close

The building itself, an 18th-century Mayfair house that spent 220 years as a home to cyclists' clubs, balloonist societies and suffragette meetings before becoming a restaurant, is left legible under the redesign rather than gutted for it

The egg-shaped white toilet pods, set beneath a barrel-vaulted ceiling tiled in dozens of stained-glass colours, commit to the same absurdist logic as the dining room instead of reverting to ordinary design once the joke could have safely stopped

The tulip-backed velvet banquettes, upholstered in the same pink as the walls, were built as bespoke furniture for the room rather than sourced off a catalogue, so the seating reads as sculpture that happens to also seat people

Even the food is drawn into the joke: dishes arrive on crockery hand-lettered with the restaurant's own street address, so the tableware keeps making the same point the walls do about a building that never stops being aware of itself
cons: A single-color room this famous photographs better than it seats: the deep booth banquettes and low lighting that make the pink glow in pictures are less comfortable for a long dinner than a conventional dining chair

The Gallery has been repainted before, swapped to sunshine yellow for a Yinka Shonibare redesign in 2022 before pink returned, which means the room diners see today is a revival rather than the original 2014 scheme

The toilet pods, however striking, function as a single-occupancy queue at peak hours, and the theatrical lighting that photographs so well up close reads as slightly clinical once the novelty of the first visit wears off

content.content: Nine Conduit Street has been many things since James Wyatt designed it as a private Mayfair residence in 1779: a townhouse, a home to a cyclists' society and a balloonists' club, a meeting place for the Suffragette movement, and for a long stretch simply a building nobody had a good use for. In 2002 the restaurateur Mourad Mazouz bought it without a clear plan beyond the conviction that a Grade II listed Georgian house deserved better than sitting empty, and turned it into sketch, a single address containing several rooms with almost nothing in common except the belief that a restaurant can also be a piece of design criticism.
https://flodeau.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/DSGallery2.jpg
content.alt: Close-up of a table set for dinner at The Gallery, sketch, London, with a blurred waiter adjusting place settings against a wall of framed David Shrigley drawings
content.caption: A table set inside the Gallery, with the Shrigley wall and one of the room's copper table lamps close enough to read individually.

content.content: One colour, no exceptions

The Gallery's most disciplined decision is the one that looks the most frivolous. India Mahdavi's 2014 redesign commits to a single millennial pink across walls, ceiling, carpet and the tulip-shaped velvet banquettes that ring the room, refusing the usual designer's instinct to break up a strong colour with a neutral counterweight. The effect is less a themed room than a habitable Rothko: from the doorway, the pink reads as one continuous surface, and only up close does it resolve into fabric, plaster, marble chevron flooring and two hundred and thirty-nine individually framed drawings. Mahdavi had three months to complete the redesign in 2014; what was originally planned as a two-year installation ran for eight.
https://flodeau.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/DS_gallery_3.jpg
content.alt: Wide-angle view of The Gallery at sketch showing pink tulip-shaped booths and chevron-patterned marble floor against walls of framed David Shrigley drawings
content.caption: The room's corner, where the herringbone marble floor meets a wall of two hundred and thirty-nine identically framed drawings.

content.content: Two hundred and thirty-nine punchlines

Those drawings are by the artist David Shrigley, whose deliberately crude, deadpan style has always worked by refusing to look expensive, which is exactly what makes it survive being hung in a room this ornamental. Gridded salon-style across every wall in identical frames, the drawings function first as texture, a uniform pattern that completes the pink room the way wallpaper would, and only on closer inspection break apart into two hundred and thirty-nine separate, absurd little jokes about failure, boredom and bad advice, the largest single body of his work ever exhibited in one place. Sketch has cycled artists through the space since, including a 2022 redesign with Yinka Shonibare that swapped the walls to sunshine yellow, but the pink Shrigley scheme was reinstated, evidence that the combination reads as the room's real identity rather than one look among several.

content.alt: Two pink-clothed tables set for dinner beneath a row of David Shrigley drawings at sketch, London, with copper table lamps and framed text-based artworks
content.caption: Individual Shrigley drawings read up close: text-based jokes hung at exactly table height.

content.content: A room built to be walked through, not just seen

Photographed empty, the Gallery can look like a stage set waiting for its cast. What the room is actually built for shows up once staff and diners are moving through it: the pink absorbs and reflects the low light so consistently that people become part of the same continuous surface as the walls and banquettes, dressed in grey uniforms that read as a deliberate, muted counterpoint rather than an oversight. Even the crockery keeps the bit going, hand-lettered in the same wry, self-referential type as the drawings, printing the restaurant's own Mayfair address onto the plate a foie gras terrine is served on, so that the joke about self-awareness reaches the food before it reaches the table.

content.alt: Foie gras terrine plated with green apple and hazelnuts on a hand-lettered plate printed with sketch's Regent Street and Conduit Street addresses
content.caption: A foie gras terrine served on crockery hand-lettered with the restaurant's own street address.

content.content: The joke that follows you downstairs

What separates sketch from a merely photogenic dining room is that the design logic doesn't stop at the door. One floor down, under a barrel-vaulted ceiling tiled edge to edge in dozens of stained-glass colours, a row of sleek white egg-shaped pods holds the restaurant's toilets, each one a private capsule glowing faintly under the coloured light spilling down from above. A weaker restaurant would treat the bathroom as an afterthought once the dining room had already done the work of being memorable; sketch treats it as one more room in the same argument, that a building can be historic, expensive, slightly ridiculous and completely serious about all three at once.
https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/630811a6ad34367560213cfa/2e47cdca-3fdd-42de-93b7-89c8885ad613/Coolest+Bathroom_Sketch+London.jpg
content.alt: Row of white egg-shaped toilet pods at sketch London beneath a barrel-vaulted ceiling tiled in dozens of stained-glass colours
content.caption: The egg-shaped toilet pods, lit from above by a ceiling tiled edge to edge in stained glass.

content.content: https://flodeau.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/07/Staff_Uniform.jpg
content.alt: Two staff members in grey uniforms standing among the egg-shaped toilet pods at sketch London, beneath a stained-glass barrel-vaulted ceiling
content.caption: Staff uniforms designed for the same room: grey against the eggs' pearl-white shells and the rainbow ceiling above.

reviews.title: Sculpture Left Out in the Fields
reviews.subject: PARK3020 · Strilky, Lviv region · Contemporary Ukrainian sculpture
reviews.author: Viacheslav Munister
reviews.meta: STRILKY, LVIV REGION · NAZAR BILYK, ZHANNA KADYROVA, OLEKSII ZOLOTAR AND OTHERS · SINCE 2020 · PHOTO: PARK3020
reviews.verdict: PARK3020 does not put sculpture on display. It puts it out in open fields, far enough apart that looking at art becomes a walk through the landscape, and a young national collection gets the room it needs to grow.
pros: The distances between the works turn every sculpture into something you approach, lose behind a rise and find again, instead of an object in a row
Commissions such as Nazar Bilyk's Space Around and Oleksii Zolotar's eight-metre Ear were made for this landscape, not moved into it
It is built as an institution, not an attraction: a partnership with Yorkshire Sculpture Park, an expert council, a symposium and a programme for young sculptors
Indoor halls add a second layer, from the 2025 Global Culture Forum to the exhibition Birth, open until 4 October 2026
cons: Without a car it takes planning: a bus from Lviv followed by a 30-minute walk
At 600 hryvnias, a standard ticket is a considered expense rather than a casual stop
The open fields that make the park work leave little shelter on hot or rainy days

content.content: Half an hour's drive from Lviv, past the village of Strilky, the land opens into long, rolling fields. Standing in them, at distances that make you walk, are a white sphere with a human profile cut into it, an eight-metre ear, a brick shell and a grove of red steel trees. This is PARK3020, the first public park of contemporary Ukrainian sculpture.

It was founded in 2020 with a clear brief: to give Ukrainian sculptors, and above all young ones, institutional, financial and educational support, a place to realise large works at home and a platform from which to be seen internationally. Six years on, the park has grown from a handful of commissions into a collection, a programme of exhibitions and an indoor art hall.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu5park3020-01.jpg
content.caption: Nazar Bilyk, Space Around, in the fields of PARK3020.

content.content: Six commissions, one field

Nazar Bilyk's Space Around is the work that has become the park's image. A human outline dissolves into the perfect form of a sphere, and with it into the space around. Bilyk, who works with the negative form of white plaster, describes these contours as both object and instrument, a way of drawing the space in which a person is present.

content.caption: Nazar Bilyk, Space Around.

content.content: Oleksii Zolotar's Ear rises eight metres out of the grass. It began, the park notes, with an unsuccessful selfie, and it addresses a familiar theme, from Bosch to Van Gogh, with an urgent one: the need to listen carefully to a world in the middle of physical war and emotional overload, and to choose what to take in. Anna Zviahintseva took a very different route to scale. Her father used to twist foil into small figures while he was thinking; she enlarged one of them, a pair of legs, to a four-metre object, turning a half-conscious habit into a monument to thought.

content.caption: Oleksii Zolotar, Ear, and Anna Zviahintseva, Sculpture of My Father.

content.content: Anton Logov's Trees of Life grow straight through the roof of a house. The landscape reminded him of the oaks of his grandparents' region near Odesa, and of the idea that to develop, a person has to cross borders and break standards. Anna Naduda's Biomorph, from the other side of the field, joins the branching form of trees to the idealised canon of ancient Greek sculpture, proposing a single form in which the bodily and the natural are the same thing.

content.caption: Anton Logov, Trees of Life, with a detail, and Anna Naduda, Biomorph.

content.content: The collection has kept growing. Zhanna Kadyrova, who tests the aesthetic potential of ordinary building materials, made a monument to a mollusc, a shell that shuts at any sign of danger, the way a person in a big city learns to. Stepan Ryabchenko's Apparition, a folded yellow column, refers to the legend of a vision said to have appeared on the site of a Kyiv botanical garden in 1862. And the GREVIS group, Volodymyr Levis and Ernest Yemeliantsev, placed a giant button in a birch clearing: a thing lost long ago that grew along with the trees, and now belongs to the landscape as much as they do.

content.caption: Zhanna Kadyrova, Shell; Stepan Ryabchenko, Apparition; GREVIS, Button.

content.content: Visiting

PARK3020 is open every day from 10:00 to 18:00, next to Edem Resort in Strilky, about 30 minutes by car from Lviv; buses 747, 842 and 843 run from Lviv bus station No. 5, followed by a 30-minute walk. Guided tours, including the exhibition halls, start at 12:00 and 15:00 and last up to two hours, and you can also walk the park on your own. A standard ticket costs 600 hryvnias; children aged 6–12, military personnel, pensioners and art students pay 300, and children under six and combat veterans enter free. Dogs are welcome, and there is parking with charging for electric cars.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/mu5park3020-19.jpg
content.caption: Late light over the fields of PARK3020.

content.content: The best way to see the park is slowly. The distances between the works are part of the experience: you approach a sculpture from far away, lose it behind a rise in the ground and find it again from another side. For a park that dates itself a thousand years ahead, it is a fitting pace.

reviews.title: Dinner Inside the North Sea
reviews.subject: Under · Bålyveien 50, Lindesnes · Snøhetta
reviews.author: Viacheslav Munister
reviews.meta: LINDESNES, NORWAY · SNØHETTA · OPENED MARCH 2019 · PHOTO: CC BY 2.0, CITY FOODSTERS / WIKIMEDIA COMMONS
reviews.verdict: Under is a thirty-four-metre concrete tube laid half into the sea at the southern tip of Norway, and it does one thing better than any dining room in Europe: it puts forty people behind an eleven-metre window, five and a half metres under the waves, and lets the North Sea decide what the view looks like tonight.
pros: The 11 × 3.4 metre underwater window is not a gimmick bolted onto a normal restaurant — the entire building is organised around reaching it, floor below floor, until the dining room is the seabed
The name is a genuine pun in Norwegian, meaning both 'below' and 'wonder,' and Snøhetta built the whole descent to earn it
The concrete shell is designed as an artificial reef, roughened to invite mussels and kelp, so the view outside the window changes and thickens with marine life year by year
A Michelin star within eight months of opening in 2019, held again in the 2026 guide under chef Bernt Sæthre — the spectacle did not end up carrying a kitchen that couldn't keep up
cons: Forty seats and one nightly seating structure mean the window itself is a scarcer resource than the tasting menu — book for the view months out, not weeks
Lindesnes is Norway's southernmost point and not on the way to anywhere: the nearest airport is Kristiansand, then close to an hour by road
A tasting menu built this far from anywhere sits at a price that assumes the building is half the reason you came, because it is

content.content: At Norway's southernmost point, where the North Sea meets the Skagerrak, a slab of dark concrete comes down out of the rocks at an angle, as if a length of pipe had been dropped from a great height and left exactly where it landed. One end is clad in raw timber and sits in the air. The other end disappears into the water. There is a door in the submerged end, underwater, sealed shut; it exists for maintenance divers, not diners. Everyone else goes in from the timber end, at the top, and walks down.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/under-exterior.jpg
content.alt: Under restaurant in Lindesnes, Norway, a long dark concrete and timber monolith built into a rocky shoreline, angled down into the sea
content.caption: Under, seen from the rocks at Lindesnes. The structure runs 34 metres from the entrance to five and a half metres below the surface.

content.content: The building is by Snøhetta, the Norwegian firm behind the Oslo Opera House, and it opened in March 2019 as Europe's first underwater restaurant, a title it still holds along with a fair claim to being the largest of its kind anywhere. The descent is the whole design idea: an entrance at sea level, a bar on a mezzanine where the concrete first meets the water, and finally the dining room itself, thirty-four metres in from the door and 5.5 metres under the surface, its long axis ending in a single window measuring eleven metres by three point four. The walls along the way are a metre of solid concrete, built to take the impact of a rough sea directly, and there is nothing between the last of the exposed timber above and the raw, unlit rock below to soften the fact that a great deal of weight is now over your head.

The name plays on that structure rather than decorating it. In Norwegian, under means both "below" and "wonder," and the building spends its entire length making the first word earn the second: you do not arrive at the wonder, you walk down into it, floor by floor, until the room itself is the seabed and the ceiling is the sea.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/under-dining.jpg
content.alt: Interior of Under restaurant's underwater dining room, tables set for dinner facing a huge panoramic window looking out into the dark blue sea, with fish visible outside
content.caption: The dining room at 5.5 metres below sea level, all forty covers facing the same eleven-metre window.

content.content: What is outside the window is not fixed scenery. Snøhetta designed the concrete shell to function as an artificial reef, its exterior deliberately roughened rather than smoothed, so that mussels, kelp and barnacles would colonise it the way they would colonise any submerged rock on this coast. Marine biologists monitor the growth from inside, and the restaurant doubles, by design, as a research station: the same window that frames dinner is also a fixed observation point on a reef that did not exist before the building did. Diners are told, more or less accurately, that no two evenings at the window look quite the same — cod and pollack pass in loose shoals, the light shifts with depth and weather, and every season adds a little more life to the concrete that wasn't there when the restaurant opened.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/under-kitchen.jpg
content.alt: Open kitchen at Under restaurant with chefs working at a counter, positioned beside the underwater window with the sea visible outside
content.caption: The open kitchen sits at the edge of the same window as the dining room — the sea is the view from both sides of the pass.

content.content: The kitchen, under founding chef Nicolai Ellitsgaard, built a tasting menu around exactly what the building was already arguing: cold-water seafood from the coast immediately outside the window, served in courses that look assembled from the shoreline itself — a single piece of scallop set into a bowl of edible black sand, mussels served in their own shells inside a woven nest of dried seaweed, langoustine and herbs plated on beach stones. Under won a Michelin star within eight months of opening, an unusually fast recognition for a restaurant this remote, and it has held one every year since; the current guide credits chef Bernt Sæthre, who has carried the kitchen forward without loosening the coastal, almost archaeological logic of the original menu.
https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/under-plate1.jpg
content.alt: A dish at Under restaurant styled to resemble a stone on a beach of dark edible sand, served on a light ceramic plate
content.caption: A course built to look like the shoreline outside the window: shellfish set into edible black sand.

content.content: https://api.eprisjournal.com/uploads/under-plate2.jpg
content.alt: Mussels served in their shells nestled inside a woven nest of dark dried seaweed on a plate at Under restaurant
content.caption: Mussels, served in a nest of dried seaweed rather than on it — the plate keeps repeating the building's argument.

content.content: It would be easy for a building this dramatic to overwhelm whatever gets served inside it, and easier still for the kitchen to lean on the view and stop trying. Under mostly avoids both traps by refusing to treat the architecture and the menu as separate arguments. The concrete is a reef; the food is what lives on a reef. The window is fixed and the sea outside it is not, and the plates keep pointing back at the same water rather than competing with it. It is a very long way to travel for dinner, at a price that assumes you know that already. But very few dining rooms anywhere are also, quietly, a piece of long-term marine research — and fewer still ask you to sit still for two hours and watch the ocean do something no camera on the wall of a normal restaurant ever could.

items.title: Овал с точками
items.subtitle: Henry Moore · 1968–70 · бронза
items.description: Два пустоты превращают бронзовый овал в меняющийся горизонт: Henry Moore придает вес, пейзаж и человеческое тело ощущаются неразделимыми.
items.homeDescription: Brandon Morris исследует границу между модой и скульптурой, создавая свою серию Ghost Dress из стекловолокна и смолы. Вдохновленный викторианской детской одеждой, фильмами ужасов такими как The Ring, а также художниками Martin Margiela, Hans Bellmer и Heidi Bucher, он представляет себе платья, существующие без тела.

items.title: Десять крупнейших, № 9, Старость
items.subtitle: Hilma af Klint · 1907 · темпера на бумаге
items.description: Hilma af Klint придает старости яркий, плавающий язык: лиловые поля, петли и темные семена делают холст ощущением выросшим, а не нарисованным.
items.homeDescription: Molly Brocklehurst — британский художник, известный своими сновидческими масляными картинами, основанными на найденных фотографиях. Ее работы исследуют память, ностальгию и размывшуюся границу между реальностью и вымыслом, создавая сцены, которые ощущаются как фрагменты забытого прошлого.

items.title: Salk Institute
items.subtitle: Louis I. Kahn · 1965 · La Jolla
items.description: В Salk Institute бетон не является фоном, а точным инструментом для света, морского воздуха и тишины.
items.homeDescription: Диалог между архитектурной историей и современным жильем. Богатые деревянные интерьеры обрамляют более тихий порядок современной мебели, создавая последовательность пространств, где материал, пропорции и тщательно контролируемые виды становятся частью опыта.

items.title: Panton Chair
items.subtitle: Verner Panton · 1960 · формованный пластик
items.description: Одна непрерывная красная линия превращается в стул: Verner Panton сводит знакомый объект к цвету, кривой и единственному безапелляционному жесту.
items.homeDescription: Скульптурный объект, построенный на напряжении между постоянством и эфемерностью. Три отлитых из стекла элемента сложены в монолитную форму, а маленькое пламя внутри добавляет тепло, движение и ощущение ритуала в иначе твердый объект.

items.title: Co-op Grain Elevator, Caldwell
items.subtitle: Russell Lee · 1940 · Caldwell, Idaho
items.description: Russell Lee превращает хранилищные башни и припаркованный трактор в тихий, почти абстрактный портрет американской инфраструктуры.
items.homeDescription: Французский фотограф Guy Bourdin преобразил модную фотографию с помощью сюрреалистических композиций, ярких цветов и загадочных повествований. Его тщательно постановочные изображения размывали границу между модой, кино и изобразительным искусством, создавая загадочные миры, которые часто больше напоминают фрагменты незавершенной истории, чем рекламу.

items.title: Сандра Кантанен: за пределами традиционной фотографии
items.subtitle: Фотография
items.description: Фотография может быть порогом, а не записью — Сандра Кантанен превращает пейзаж в пространство между памятью, мифом и оптическим искажением.
items.homeSubtitle: Федора Э. Д. Браун · около 1908 · желатино-серебряный отпечаток
items.homeDescription: Тропа растворяется в дымке и деревьях, превращая пейзаж в память, которая ещё наводит резкость.
items.homeCredit: Федора Э. Д. Браун · общественное достояние / Wikimedia Commons
items.homeLabel: Федора Э. Д. Браун · около 1908 · желатино-серебряный отпечаток

items.title: Против прямого угла
items.subtitle: Architecture
items.description: Пять зданий, которые выговорили себе свободу от сетки, — и софт, металл, деньги и чистая наглость, которые понадобились, чтобы их построить.
items.homeDescription: Тихий бетонный каркас превращает погоду, повторение и низкий горизонт в одну выверенную композицию.

items.title: Утренние ритуалы
items.subtitle: Каппадокия, Турция
items.description: Тишина рассвета и вкус свежего кофе с видом на долины.

items.title: Городское одиночество
items.subtitle: Берлин, Германия
items.description: Нахождение покоя в конкретном ритме города.

items.title: Средиземноморский праздник
items.subtitle: Сицилия, Италия
items.description: Праздник простых ингредиентов: оливкового масла, помидоров и морской соли.

items.title: Горное дыхание
items.subtitle: Карпаты, Украина
items.description: Свежий воздух высокогорья и аромат соснового леса.

items.title: Искусство, которое заставляет вас улыбаться
items.subtitle: Красочные и игривые предметы обладают уникальным качеством, которого нет у других: они привносят в комнату чистое счастье.
items.description: Я считаю, что когда вы вводите в окружающую среду игровые предметы, это расширяет границы разума. Это дает вам невербальное разрешение мыслить свободно – не только отвергать общепринятые рамки, но и забывать о их существовании.
items.homeDescription: Тело становится скоростью: Боччони превращает фигуру в единый аэродинамический жест между скульптурой и полётом.
items.homeCredit: Умберто Боччони · общественное достояние / Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Тадао Андо: расшифровка философии чистого дизайна
items.subtitle: Архитектура
items.description: Тадао Андо — один из самых влиятельных архитекторов XXI века, бросающий вызов привычным границам архитектуры. Его подход переосмысляет традиционные японские принципы через смелые формы, материалы и организацию пространства. В статье — ключевые принципы его философии.

items.title: Польский дизайн: соткан из памяти
items.subtitle: Дизайн
items.description: Современный польский дизайн переживает момент тихой зрелости. В студиях сегодняшних архитекторов и мебельщиков говорят на языке строгого минимализма, тактильных материалов и честной конструкции — итог векового диалога о том, что значит творить с национальной душой.
items.homeDescription: Простой лист становится плавным сиденьем: повседневный материал превращается в скульптурную и удивительно щедрую форму.
items.homeCredit: Фрэнк Гери · фото CC0 / Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Сердце EPRIS: у Марии диплом архитектора
items.subtitle: Culture
items.description: 7 июля Мария Иванова, главный редактор EPRIS, официально получила степень бакалавра архитектуры. Чтобы отметить этот день – сердце, построенное из архитектуры и искусства, которые ее вдохновляют.

items.title: Как Эмили Краус заново изобретает живопись

items.homeSubtitle: Хильма аф Клинт · 1907 · темпера на бумаге
items.homeDescription: Сиреневые поля, солнечные диаграммы и тёмное семя в центре делают картину похожей не на холст, а на рост из невидимого космоса.
